#9748. Dutch data protection authority advises against purchasing AI camera glasses

Monique Verdier, Deputy Chair of the AP: “Glasses that film you without your knowledge are already a cause for concern. Glasses that also give you the wrong advice when someone’s life is at stake go a step too far. AI offers many opportunities, provided that we are able to trust that technology. In the case of the camera glasses that we examined, that trust cannot be justified at present.”

The AP investigated six AI camera glasses available on the Dutch market. Two of these were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations in which people’s safety was a key consideration.

The results are alarming. During a simulated emergency in which advice on CPR was sought, one of the glasses claimed on several occasions that an ambulance was already on its way, even though no emergency services had been called. In a real emergency, such an error could result in essential help arriving too late, with potentially life-threatening consequences.

The AI camera glasses also made errors related to the protection of minors, with potentially very serious consequences. For example, one pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who was interested in a minor. In another test, safety warnings on toys for young children were not followed. The glasses also made mistakes when reading medicine leaflets and interpreting warnings about extreme weather.

The tests show that AI camera glasses can sound convincing, even if the information provided is incorrect or even dangerous. As a result, users may wrongly rely on advice that is not safe.

In addition to these safety risks, the AP identified serious shortcomings in the protection of personal data. The recording lights on nearly all the camera glasses examined were barely visible and easy to cover up. Most glasses continued to film after the lights were covered, even though the manufacturer claimed this should not be possible. As a result, bystanders can hardly see whether they are being filmed.

Often, it is also unclear what happens to the footage and audio recordings. The AI functions examined process data through external servers, often located outside the European Union. Users are not provided with sufficient information about the AI models that process their data and the companies they share these data with. Furthermore, the AP discovered serious security issues with several pairs of glasses. As a result, someone nearby could connect to the glasses without permission, view recordings or even control the camera.

The AP currently considers AI camera glasses to be unsafe because of the risks they pose to users and bystanders. The AP therefore advises consumers against buying AI camera glasses at this stage.However, the AP also recognises several legitimate uses for the technology. AI camera glasses can be valuable for people who are visually impaired or have low literacy levels, or who otherwise need support to understand their surroundings. But it is precisely for these users that it is important for the technology to be reliable.

The AP calls on Dutch and European policymakers to include these new research findings in the further development of policies on AI camera glasses. “It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these kinds of high-risk AI products. Simply banning everything provides some breathing space for now, but we cannot keep this up indefinitely. It is essential that we work collectively to raise awareness, build resilience and foster ethical consciousness,” says Monique Verdier.

The AP recommends that owners and managers of locations prohibit the wearing and use of camera glasses in their house rules (in Dutch).

#9746. Training a coding model to paint watercolours with TRL and OpenEnv

On 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model. The model writes JavaScript through p5.brush, a library that "adds natural drawing tools to p5.js". The video went viral fast, over 1.5M views at the time of writing.

The video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet. His site says a full technical report is coming, so ensure you follow him. The original idea is his, coming from the art and design side, where his skills are way beyond mine. My attempt is on the engineering side, reproducing the recipe in the open with every piece published.

Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.

In this article I try and reproduce his idea with TRL and OpenEnv. The reference pool dataset, the RL environment, the training scripts and the trained models, all open.

The whole pipeline runs on Hugging Face, end to end:

Once the two Spaces are up, the recipe is one command. Duplicate the environment and the scorer model, set two environment variables for the reward mix, and launch:

The rest of this article is the story of getting there, and every piece is in the repo.

I have followed the original blog step by step, and only changed something when strictly needed. Every idea of my own went into a list instead of into the experiment, and that list became "What I would try next" at the end, next to the full list of published artifacts. If you have already read his post, the framing and the reward design will be familiar. The new material is the open implementation, the hand-rated pool, and three reward mixes trained and compared, and it starts at The RL environment you need to build.

The paintings look loose, imperfect, handmade, at a moment when image models produce perfect (statistically average) pictures. My guess is that this contrast is a big part of why the video went viral. It reminded me of the early days of generative AI art, when the point was to explore the medium. DeepDream (2015) was a debugging tool that people turned into art, works like Edmond de Belamy (2018) came from artists probing what a GAN could do, and artists like Mario Klingemann spent those years making dreamy portraits with neural networks.

This project feels closer to those early days. In his thesis, Surya describes the path that led here. He started by prompting text-to-image models, where the prompt is the only lever you can pull, and more detail buys more control only up to a point. Training the model itself goes further. The other half of the idea is the medium. The model writes a program of about 150 lines of JavaScript that paints the image. That model output is code. You can read it, edit it and run it again, and the decision behind each brushstroke is visible. And the style comes from a restriction where the model is only allowed ten of the library's methods. More on that below.

In that same period, Anna Ridler photographed thousands of tulips, hand-labelled every one, exhibited the dataset itself as the artwork, and later trained a model on it. I found her work through the references AI agents brought back while building this project and loved it because this project does something very similar by curating a set of images by hand, and then training against them.

Most of the recent RL work on language models uses rewards you can verify. For example, math problems with a known answer, code that passes tests, or graders that are right or wrong and cheap to run. This project is closer to the older exception, RLHF, where the model learns a reward model from human preferences.

Here the reward is aesthetic preference. There is no correct answer. The real question of the project is whether you can do RL over taste.

The reward, as his blog defines it and as the RL environment I built implements it:

HPSv3 is an open 7B preference model. Give it an image and a text description, and it returns a score for how much a person would prefer that image. It was trained on a large set of human choices between pairs of images, so its score is an average of many people's taste. The pairwise judge is Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, a general vision model called through HF Inference Providers. The pairwise judge sees the candidate painting next to four references randomly selected from the pool, guided by a written description of what to weigh (bleeds, translucent washes, soft edges), each comparison in both presentation orders, and its score is the share of comparisons the candidate wins. Its only standard is the pool, so its score is my taste, as encoded in those ratings.

Those are the weights Narreddi converged on. The pool defines taste here. That moves the work from tuning hyperparameters to building the set that decides what is beautiful.

I trained three runs with this reward. They differ only in how the weight splits between the two model judges:

I started with hps-only to validate that the pipeline could learn at all. Once the reward was going up and the metrics were healthy, there was no reason to run it longer, so I launched the two longer runs instead. The question that the longer runs ask is how much of HPSv3's power can you hand to the pairwise judge? The more weight the judge carries, the more the reward means my taste instead of everyone's, and the harder it should be to climb. Incidentally, if you push it far enough or your style is too far from the average, the model could stop entirely.

Fortunately, it did not stop and both runs with the pairwise judge on learned too. The hand-rated pool can steer the policy, at least as far as the metrics and the final paintings show. The numbers are below.

Disclaimer. If we use a frontier model, it can already generate the JavaScript code that paints watercolour from a prompt. That's the starting point. The work here is about teaching a smaller model to do it combined with a person's own artistic preferences.

The environment wraps everything that sits between the model and the reward, including the JavaScript library that the model uses for painting, the system prompt that restricts it, the headless Chromium that renders each sketch, and the gate that rejects cheats.

The library does more of the work than it seems. p5.brush, by @acamposuribe, simulates a medium rather than drawing shapes: pigment bleeds past the edges of a fill, paper has texture, strokes have mass, flow fields drag brushwork around. When the model calls brush.fillBleed(0.25) it is deciding how far the ink runs.

Note. The author of p5.brush had been trying to teach a machine to paint long before any of this. In 2022 he made a generative art series that hides a diary about teaching p5.js to draw like a child: "It is barely able to use the crayons [...] It cannot follow simple commands. I'm done for today, very infuriating." The series was meant to have three pieces, and he made two. When Surya's video went viral, he quoted it, sharing that diary and saying this work is the third piece arriving on its own.

p5.brush exposes 47 methods. The prompt allows 10: scaleBrushes, noStroke, fill, noFill, fillBleed, fillTexture, beginShape, vertex, endShape and circle. What the other thirty-seven add, lines, hatching, custom brushes, would break the watercolour look. With these ten the model can only paint filled shapes, and the library adds the bleed to every one of them.

His blog post saved me a lot of time I could have wasted iterating on the prompt. A long API reference makes the model invent methods that do not exist, and his 200 GEPA iterations converged on a strict allowlist with no documentation. I saw the same failures and wrote the allowlist by hand. My only addition to that recipe is one sentence: paint each petal two or three times, a big pass first and a smaller, more opaque one inside it. This small change made my outputs a lot more colorful.

Note. If it's the first time you hear about GEPA, it is an automatic prompt optimizer. A language model reflects in plain words on where the current prompt failed and proposes a better one, and the loop repeats.

The gate is the final piece. The sketch has to compile, use the library instead of direct p5 calls, put real pigment on the canvas, and not try to trick the scorer, for example by writing text on the canvas.

The pool consists of 178 paintings divided into two tiers based on my personal preferences, love and okay. All of them are actually generated by a model. Four open-weight models, called through Inference Providers, wrote p5.brush sketches, each one working from a real, openly licensed photo of a hibiscus from iNaturalist. A vision model gave written feedback on every sketch, over three refinement iterations. Every final render was then rated one at a time, by me, and 178 made the cut.

Here I chose four different families of models to test their different styles. These four were the open models that produced a valid sketch every time in a quick reliability check, and two other candidates were dropped for failing it. If you want to produce your own pool, you might choose others.

The tiers do real work in the reward. When the pairwise judge draws four references, half come from love and half from okay, so the policy always faces some rivals it can sometimes beat, and a win pays the same against either tier. This is one of my few deliberate changes: the original compares against its top tier only, and I kept the easier tier in the draw so a weak early policy still gets signal.

No human-made painting is in there, which is a real limitation. p5.brush is a niche library, and the human work that exists in it with accessible code is a handful of pieces, nowhere near what a training corpus would need, as his blog also notes.

The interesting idea here, as I've already discussed previously, is that the model will learn to imitate what the pool contains. If we point the environment at a different dataset, the reward would automatically change without touching a single line of code. For the dataset I generated and openly share, I also include the source sketch.

If we look closer at the judges, the two of them answer different questions. HPSv3 decides whether it is a flower, and the pairwise judge decides whether it is well painted in the style I chose.

Before anything worked, there was a long stretch of flat reward curves. If you've tried to reproduce a research paper/blog without open artifacts, you probably can relate. Every run tested what I thought was a reasonable theory about what was wrong. A run takes a lot of time, so I queued the next one while still going through the last one's results. As always, starting from something easier that works and then building on top of that was the answer. A simple control task, with no browser and no judges, was the first attempt that learned, and the reason was that my learning rate was just too low.

Another change that cost me time to find was adjusting the LoRA parameters correctly. The usual target_modules list assumes a dense model, and Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a mixture of experts that names most of its projections differently, so the adapter was training ten layers out of forty. I solved this by changing it to all-linear, which reaches every linear layer. The routed experts in this architecture are fused tensors that even all-linear leaves frozen, but everything else gets an adapter, and that was enough to learn.

The fix was four changes in TRL's GRPOTrainer:

These four changes unlocked the first successful run (hps-only), with the reward clearly improving.

With that configuration, all three runs learn. Both judge runs were launched for 200 steps and stopped at 110, with the reward still climbing slowly. A step takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, and the comparison between mixes was already stable, so I stopped both to save compute. Mean group reward over the first and final third of each run:

The three curves line up with how much weight my taste carries. The more the judge weighs, the lower the start and the noisier the climb. judge-led spent its first thirty steps nearly flat before it moved. It is the same move that solved the debugging. Shrink the problem until something learns, then add the hard parts back one at a time.

The pairwise judge term itself climbed in the two runs that used it. The model wins more comparisons against the pool as training advances, which is the claim hps-only could not make. No group in any run collapsed to identical rewards, the GRPO failure mode that kills the gradient. For the curious, the per-metric curves (HPSv3, paint coverage, entropy) are in the repository as CSV.

The full launch command, the hardware and the two environment variables that turn this into the other two runs are in the recipe.

In every run, the first thing the model learned was to stop producing bad paintings, the near-blank canvases and shapeless washes that score under 0.3 in total reward. In hps-only, three quarters of the rise in the group mean comes from bad paintings becoming rare. In the judge runs the collapse is even steeper: rollouts under 0.3 fall from 99 to 16 across judge-led's thirds, and from 37 to 4 in hps-led.

This is why the obvious visual, the best painting of each step, shows almost no difference in hps-only. It moves +0.034 across the run while the median moves +0.155. The learning is visible in the middle of the distribution.

What the pairwise judge changes is the top. In hps-only, paintings got more reliable without getting better. The quality of the good ones added just +0.03 to the group mean, and once HPSv3 saw petals around a centre and a stem, it stopped asking for more pigment. With the judge on, the other half of the story appears. Better here means closer to the pool, so closer to what I rated as "good" or something I liked more. That added +0.12 in judge-led and +0.16 in hps-led, the best of each step rose too, and paint coverage doubled in both runs (0.11 to 0.23, and 0.13 to 0.30) where hps-only barely moved it. With a reference left to beat, a good painting can still get better, and the model starts being rewarded for using more pigment.

One more finding. The model ignores an explicit instruction, and it is right to. The system prompt asks for fifteen to thirty filled shapes. If we look at the real mean, it is between 7 and 9, and n_shapes barely correlates with reward in any run (+0.000, −0.14, +0.07). The policy is not rewarded for obeying that sentence, so it does not obey it.

There is also a ceiling on the hps-only route. If every rollout matched its good ones, that run's mean would sit at 0.771. Whether more steps would break it is an open question.

The paintings also show something that the tables miss. Within each run, they all look similar. As training advances, the rewards inside each group get closer together, and the median paintings in the opening video look like takes of the same flower. That is GRPO doing what it is designed to do with a pool built from one subject. The pool decides what counts as variety, the same way it decides what counts as quality. If the reward only pays for matching one flower, the model learns to paint that one flower. More diverse output would need a more diverse pool, and building one is more curation work. Surya's newer compositions are an example of this. Alex Yango's animal paintings are the same recipe with different choices in the pool. This is the biggest difference between an aesthetic reward and a maths grader. Behind the number there is a very human job, deciding what belongs in the reward set. Jason Liu's essay on taste says the general version in one line. AI shifted the bottleneck from making to noticing.

Surya closes his blog with some of his favourites. Instead of picking mine, below is a wall with the 178 paintings the reward scored highest across the two judge runs, the same number the reference pool holds, in no particular order. Open it and pick your own.

To choose, you looked at many and kept a few, and that is exactly the job that built the reward of this project. Every painting of every run, with its sketch and its reward, is in the rollouts datasets, and browsable in this gallery.

Since the reward was partly based on my taste, it is fair to close with my verdict as a viewer. To my eye, judge-led is the run that ends up the most diverse and the most artistically interesting. hps-led paints convincing watercolours, but its best ones share a soft, wet-on-wet look that is almost a style of its own. hps-only converges the hardest, and most of its paintings settle on the same colours. You can judge for yourself in the gallery, which has every painting of every run, sortable by step and by reward.

This project is mostly infra. A run needs a trainer, two Spaces, an inference router and a websocket to stay healthy for hours straight, and every piece that fails quietly turns into a wrong number somewhere else. Half the work is checking that the number you read matches what actually happened.

Failures of the infrastructure were entering the reward as zeros. A render that timed out or a scorer that did not answer scored the same as a bad painting, 0.0 inside the group. Across all my runs that was about 1.5% of rollouts, and in the worst run it reached 5.2%. That trains the model on noise, so those paths now return None and the rollout is excluded from the group.

I also found a bug in OpenEnv, and sent the fix upstream. The client keeps one persistent websocket, and a socket closed by the far end stayed cached, so every later call failed even though the environment was healthy. It cost me two half-finished runs to find it. The fix is submitted upstream, and the runs launched with it have been running clean since.

The reward of a step depends on which references it drew. The pairwise judge samples four references per step, so every step faces a different set of rivals, and some draws are simply harder. GRPO itself is mostly safe, because advantages are computed inside the group and a hard draw moves the whole group together. The curve I was reading was not safe, and some of what looked like a bad step was just a hard draw. The image above is one example. Step 12 scored half a point below step 11 mostly because it drew the hardest references of the run, while the paintings themselves look close.

Rounded numbers, and only for the runs that finished.

A step is eight rollouts and takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, of which 70 to 80% is rendering. A single render takes 69 to 96 seconds against a 90 second deadline. Part of that is expected, the Space has no GPU, so Chromium renders the WEBGL canvas in software and p5.brush's bleeds and textures are heavy pixel work. Even so, I expected it to be faster, and I have not found the full cause.

A scorer can cost more than the training that uses it: HPSv3 has to be up for the whole run, so pause the Space, or set its sleep timer, when the run ends.

Everything runs on HF Jobs, with the environment as a Docker Space and metrics in trackio.

The rule of this project was to reproduce the recipe with every resource open, not to improve it, so a list of untried ideas piled up along the way. These are the ones I would actually try, in order of how much evidence there is.

Multi-step, and letting the model see what it paints. This is the first thing I would try. The original blog trains single turn, so I trained single turn, and in this setup the model paints with its eyes closed. No image ever goes in, and the only feedback it gets is one number. The evidence that a feedback loop works is the pool itself. The reference paintings came from models iterating three rounds under a vision critic, and the later rounds are better. The material that defines the reward was made with a loop the policy never gets.

Smaller models. There is evidence that 35B is more than needed. In my side experiments a 4B already wrote valid sketches that passed the gate. If a 4B can learn this, the cost of the experiment drops by an order of magnitude.

Other ideas on the list are SFT on the pool sources before starting RL, rewarding pigment explicitly, moving the judge's reference mix from easy to hard as the run advances until only love remains, widening the ten-method allowlist for more visual range (my attempts on this crashed more sketches and broke the watercolour look), and checking how consistent the pairwise judge really is by scoring the same image twice.

And the method is not specific to flowers. Alex Yango painted animals with the same mechanism, and Brendan Hogan trained canvas animations against a pool of hand-rated clips. I had also played with something similar before using Simon Willison's pelican benchmark, where code is rendered to an image and scored.

And underneath all of it sits the question this project cannot close. 178 paintings made by models define what this trained model considers beautiful. The pool is the bottleneck, and it is the part of the pipeline with no principled answer.

For anyone reproducing this, there are two deliberate divergences from Narreddi's recipe, both argued earlier in the article:

The rest, all-linear for the LoRA, infrastructure failures returning None instead of 0.0, stopping the judge runs at step 110, are decisions I had to make along the way because his blog does not specify them. His implementation is not published, so I cannot tell whether they match his choices or diverge from them.

The per-rollout numbers in this article can be recomputed from the published datasets. Nothing here depends on any Space staying switched on.

The method and original idea are Surya Narreddi's. The library is Alejandro Campos Uribe's.

#9745. Microsoft brings serverless PostgreSQL into Fabric to bridge transactions and analytics

HorizonDB preview follows rivals' moves, with analysts warning tighter integration could make an eventual exit harder

Microsoft has brought its HorizonDB PostgreSQL service into public preview in Fabric, aiming to bring transactional and analytical workloads closer together.

The corporation says applications can submit queries through a single PostgreSQL endpoint, with transactional and analytical work handled by the appropriate engines.

Analysts said the move follows similar efforts by Databricks and Snowflake to combine operational databases with analytics. But tighter integration with Microsoft's stack could make applications harder to move elsewhere.

Fabric HorizonDB joins SQL database and Cosmos DB in Microsoft's Fabric database portfolio. "By bringing operational databases, analytics, and AI together on a unified, governed platform, developers can build intelligent applications with less data movement and complexity. Fabric HorizonDB will also serve as the PostgreSQL backend for Fabric apps," Microsoft said.

Microsoft first unveiled Azure HorizonDB in preview in November 2025 and made it generally available last week. It competes with other cloud database services and distributed systems such as CockroachDB and YugabyteDB, both of which support PostgreSQL's wire protocol.

At the time, it said HorizonDB would offer "massive read scale without the need to replicate the database between instances."

Speaking to The Register last week, Shireesh Thota, veep of Azure databases and Fabric applications, said that bringing the system into Fabric – its platform for data lakes, data warehouses, and analytics launched in 2023 – would connect operational data in HorizonDB with analytical data in OneLake, Fabric's unified data lake.

"Once the data hits the OneLake storage, you can have analytical engines that take advantage of it. In HorizonDB, the PostgreSQL query engine can talk to the distributed query engine that we use in our Fabric data warehouse. We're fusing these query engines, thereby enabling the developers to submit a query that has pieces of the query that can work on OLTP and pieces of the query that can work on OLAP," he said.

"The application need not worry about two endpoints, or about consistency of data and all that complexity. They can just talk to HorizonDB as a Fabric endpoint, and they can submit all these queries. We are basically operationalizing in OneLake."

Operational data remains in HorizonDB's database storage, while mirroring maintains an analytical copy in OneLake, introduced in 2023, which replicates a snapshot of the external database to OneLake in Delta Parquet tables and keeps the replica synced in "near real time."

Thota said the process would not affect the transactional system. "Our core goal is to never impact OLTP workload while we are doing this, and we succeed [by] reading off the log as an additional replica to do this mirroring," he said.

But the overall plan of putting serverless PostgreSQL OLTP in an analytics platform, bringing it close to OLAP systems, is one some vendors are already executing to meet the demands of new AI agent-led workloads.

Adam Ronthal, research veep in Gartner's Data and Analytics Group, said: "The addition of Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB follows the 2025 acquisitions of PostgreSQL vendors by Databricks – Neon – and Snowflake – Crunchy. It delivers a high-performance, serverless operational RDBMS that is tightly coupled with Microsoft's lakehouse offering and well-suited to the ephemeral demands of AI agents.

"Competing directly with AWS Aurora and Google Cloud's AlloyDB, HorizonDB acts as a foundational serving layer for the next generation of AI- and analytics-infused applications. For organizations aligned with Azure and Fabric, it provides an industry-standard PostgreSQL foundation for AI development."

Andrew Snodgrass, research vice president of analyst company Directions on Microsoft, said the announcement of HorizonDB in Fabric was a "surprise," although "a watered-down version" compared to the version of the serverless database that became generally available on Azure last week. "It joins (document database) CosmosDB in Fabric and SQL database (based on the SQL Server engine) in Fabric. It highlights that Microsoft is still focused on making Fabric the data hub of their universe."

HorizonDB – both in Azure and Fabric – is a PostgreSQL service which Microsoft says has 100 percent compatibility with the open source system that has enjoyed a meteoric rise over the last decade. The support for PostgreSQL has led some to question the software giant's commitment to its own proprietary OLTP system, SQL Server.

Thota pointed out that the SQL database, based on the SQL Server engine, is already available in Fabric. Microsoft is also evaluating similar integration for that service, although he gave no timetable. "We are just beginning this journey, and most of the innovation is neutral to PostgreSQL and SQL. Some of it would be particular to how the individual query engine fuses with the analytical query engine. PostgreSQL does it slightly differently than SQL, but the idea is that most of the work is neutral. We are evaluating that work as well. I don't have timelines for that, but it is certainly in our thinking," he said.

Nonetheless, Holger Mueller, principal analyst at Constellation Research, said it was good to see Microsoft go all in on support of open source. "In general, it is an acknowledgement that they cannot win the battle for the SQL database with SQL Server – as it is as proprietary as the leader Oracle – and now they bank on the openness of PostgreSQL as another approach," he said.

However, using HorizonDB integrated into the Fabric/Azure stack may create so many dependencies with Microsoft's technology that lock-in to the vendor will remain a risk. "The primary concerns of open source – scale and support – have been eliminated by Microsoft's commitment and by now track record... the challenges are the embeddings of HorizonDB into the bigger Microsoft stack – which will make portability hard again. But every vendor wants and provides stickiness – clothed in ease of use and lower TCO," Mueller said. ®

#9744. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with new runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

From there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the new one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and shows exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three important properties:

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:

Or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:

funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent says so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

Published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious

Your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

#9742. Nightmare mode: simulating disk failures

November 24, 2026 | Anjana Ratnayake, Forward deployed engineer | Teymour Aldridge, Forward deployed engineer

Monthly reliability and distributed systems news, curated for teams building critical software.

Please enable JavaScript in your browser to load and submit this form.

Check your inbox for your confirmation message.

We couldnât submit your form. Please try again later.

Building a correct distributed system is really, really hard. Building a correct distributed system that has to store data and never lose it is even harder.

Many of our customers build systems where storing data reliably is paramount. Storage is hard even when nothing goes wrong. For example, some customers watch how full their disks are and compact data when necessary to reclaim space, and shard it across machines before any one disk hits its limits. Some maintain a write-ahead log so they can recover from a process restart. Others rely on a careful sequence of operations to guarantee durability and atomicity, for example writing a new copy of a file and renaming it over the old one, so that a change happens completely or not at all.

Unfortunately, storage devices are unreliable, which only adds further complexity to every interaction with the disk. Consider a single write. If it fails with an error, the system has to decide whether it is safe to retry or whether it has to give up. If it fails because the disk is out of space, the system may have to trigger compaction before it can continue. Even creating a file can fail because the filesystem has run out of inodes, and the system then has to delete other files to make room.

Moreover, unreliability can come in the form of latency. A disk can be slow, for example because of I/O contention or a failing device, which can then stretch operations out so they overlap in ways they normally wouldnât. If a read and a write end up happening at the same time, the reader may see the old data, the new data, or a random interleaving of the two.

Complexity also arises once you assume the disk will not always be there. If a write succeeds and the machine loses power immediately afterwards, a read after the restart could see all of the data, a random part of it, or none of it.

On the Antithesis Forward Deployed Engineering team, weâve had recurring discussions with customers who build this critical software, and who would like to inject disk faults or storage errors during their Antithesis simulations to mimic these kinds of situations and to ensure their software can handle it. One of the first things we realized is that different customers had vastly different expectations of their storage, and of the guarantees it should provide. This was further complicated by some running on the ext4 filesystem, and some on XFS or ZFS, each with its own behaviors under failure.

This diversity of requirements has made it hard to build a one-size-fits-all solution up front. Instead, we worked with individual customers to build several solutions, geared to their specific use cases. For instance, to test space reclamation logic weâd simulate filling up the whole filesystem.

Other approaches include shouting at the disks.

Once weâd got a sense of the requirements of different customers, we worked to incorporate these pieces of the puzzle into a comprehensive filesystem fault injection mechanism. In this post, weâll give a tour of the disk faults that a ânightmare modeâ fault injector needs to be able to emulate. Weâll start with the fault everyone asks for first, power failure, and explain what it took to emulate it convincingly. From there weâll get into the subtler things a disk can do: torn writes, I/O errors (including the one behind the fsyncgate bug), and the latency faults that shake out concurrency bugs.

Before we get into faults, weâll give some background on how file writes work in the âhappy pathâ case.

When a program writes to a file, the data does not go to disk right away. Instead, it goes into the kernelâs page cache. The kernel then writes it to disk on its own schedule, through a process called writeback. If a program needs the data on disk immediately, it can call fsync, which tells the kernel to write that fileâs data to disk and doesnât return until the write has finished. Data that is written but not fsynced could be destroyed by a power loss.

The diagram below shows these steps for a successful write to disk:

Now letâs start looking at what happens when things go wrong. We started with power loss because it seemed like the fault most of our customers would care about.

Antithesis already has a related fault type, node kills, which randomly SIGKILL a container. The SIGKILL destroys the process, but has no effect on the machine, which keeps running, so the kernel and its page cache carry on as if nothing happened. Every write the process completed still makes its way to disk, fsync or no fsync, courtesy of the kernelâs writeback mechanism. As far as the process is concerned, a SIGKILL is a fairly polite way to die, since you only lose data that the process never handed to the kernel.

The diagram below shows how data that was written but never fsynced survives the SIGKILL and lands on disk anyway:

A power failure is less polite. It loses everything the kernel accepted but hadnât synced yet. Data that has been written but not yet fsynced is simply gone:

Unfortunately, when weâre simulating faults in Antithesis, we canât just pull the plug on the machine. So the next best option was to fake it. That meant dealing with the two things that stop a container kill from causing data or cache loss: the kernelâs page cache, which holds on to unsynced data, and the kernelâs writeback, which saves unsynced data to disk.

The problem was that both of these live inside the kernel, out of our reach. Currently, there is no way to ask the kernel to forget whatâs in its cache, or to stop the kernelâs automatic writeback. However, we found a way around this: LazyFS, an open-source filesystem from INESC TEC and Jepsen.

LazyFS uses FUSE, a Linux feature that lets a userspace program act as a filesystem. Because every read and write goes through LazyFS, it can hold written data in its own internal cache, emulating the kernelâs page cache in user space. Writes to LazyFS stay in the internal cache until the program calls fsync, and only then does LazyFS write it to persistent storage. Also, there is no background writeback to save it in the meantime. This gives us the ability to âforgetâ unsynced data at any convenient moment, simply by clearing the cache. If we do that at the same moment we kill the application, the two together are indistinguishable from a real power loss.

Hereâs a diagram of we can use LazyFS to emulate power loss:

Before settling on FUSE, we looked at a couple of other mechanisms for injecting faults. eBPF was tempting, since it makes some faults, like returning a particular error code from a syscall, easy to implement. However, it would be difficult to emulate power failure, since it only allows us to watch and tweak calls as they go by. It canât hold on to data and release it (or lose it) later, which is the trick we needed. We also thought about using a custom block device, but that had the opposite problem: it can hold data, but it sits at the wrong level of abstraction. Since itâs below the filesystem, it sees blocks rather than syscalls, which makes syscall-level faults hard to implement. Power loss is especially tricky because you canât tell data that arrived through an fsync from data the kernelâs writeback happened to push out. That would cost us the strictness that catches missing fsyncs.

So LazyFS was very useful to us, and we want to extend a thank you to the authors for writing such a high quality tool. We ran a patched version (extended with additional fault types) for a while on a number of customer tenants, and it found some subtle data loss bugs.

After that, we decided to implement our own FUSE filesystem: Amnesia. We wanted to move to Rust for its memory safety, and to rework the design so the model was simpler and faster, since we planned to build a lot more on top of it.

For instance, Amnesia works directly on inodes, whereas LazyFS uses the path for every operation and has to map it back to the inode. Since a path is only a name for a file, this makes operations like renames, hard links, and deleting a file that is still open awkward to track. Working with inodes instead makes that complexity disappear. Amnesia also never touches a real disk. LazyFS writes synced data through to the backing filesystem. Amnesia keeps both the volatile state and the âdurableâ state in memory, which allows us to model an fsync as a bookkeeping update instead of another real I/O. This makes it much faster, and just as safe, because the machine never actually loses power. We made a number of other changes too, which we will get into below.

Beyond the design, LazyFS introduced us to the subtler effects of a real power loss: torn writes and torn sequences of writes, both caused by the fact that the kernel and the disk do not persist data in the order or the units a program might expect.

The LazyFS paper by Ramos et al. is a good read if you want the details.

It also made us aware of the wrinkles of working at the FUSE layer. For instance, the kernel page cache still sits in front of the FUSE filesystem, and it can be holding copies of the data we just âlostâ by emulating a power failure. Thankfully, LazyFS had already worked out the right FUSE settings and patterns to make sure the program never sees them.

Building on FUSE made it easy to add disk I/O errors, another fault type that our customers wanted. The obvious approach is to simply return the error, and that model alone was enough to find some bugs. But because we emulate the kernel page cache, we can sometimes apply the possible side effects of these errors to it, which gives us a higher degree of fidelity.

Out of the box, LazyFS does not simulate disk I/O errors as a form of fault injection, so this was new ground for us. We added the ability to return a few disk I/O error types on syscalls. One of the most interesting ones was EIO (âError: Input/Outputâ, the generic âdisk failedâ error) on fsync.

This error can interact with the kernel page cache in surprising ways. This is exactly whatâs behind the infamous fsyncgate bug. The discovery led to PostgreSQL fixing how it handles a failed fsync (it now crashes and recovers from its log rather than trying again), and it changed how the rest of us read fsyncâs promise for good. As Craig Ringer, the PostgreSQL developer who reported the problem, put it:

When fsync() returns success it means âall writes since the last fsync have hit diskâ but we assume it means âall writes since the last SUCCESSFUL fsync have hit diskâ.

To understand why Craig is correct, we need some background on what happens during an fsync on a typical Linux filesystem such as ext4. The kernelâs page cache holds file data in fixed-size chunks called pages, and marks a page as âdirtyâ when it has been changed but not yet written to disk. When a program calls fsync, the kernel sends each of the fileâs dirty pages to the storage device through a driver. Crucially, the kernel clears a pageâs dirty flag before handing it off. The fsync then waits for the driver to report whether each write succeeded.

Now suppose one of those writes to the device fails. The fsync will then return EIO, but nothing goes back and marks the page dirty again. As far as the kernel is concerned, that page is now clean, so neither the next fsync nor the background writeback will ever try to submit it to the device again. Since there are no dirty pages associated with the file, the next fsync succeeds. Unless the program happens to write the same data again and re-dirties the pages, that data never reaches the disk.

We can emulate this scenario in the FUSE layer. When the fault fires, fsync returns EIO and the affected pages are marked clean in our internal cache, without being written to persistent storage. A retried fsync then succeeds, but the data will be lost at the next emulated power failure unless the program writes it again and calls fsync.

Building on FUSE also let us add âdisk latencyâ, another commonly requested fault type.

Disk latency is really about finding concurrency bugs. Talking to the disk can be slow and unpredictable, and programs that assume otherwise can have races. These races can occur for several reasons. For example, data may land on the disk in an unpredictable order, or land in the kernel page cache in pieces rather than all at once. So we wanted to make those races easier to find.

We currently support two kinds of latency fault:

Completing operations out of order. Instead of answering syscalls in the order they arrive, we let the fuzzer decide the order they complete in.

Since Amnesia sits underneath the program and sees every operation as a request, it can decide whether to answer immediately or hold on to the request. For instance, when data from a write operation arrives, we sometimes hold onto it with a deadline while other operations continue to be processed (the deadline provides a backstop: once it passes, the operation finishes no matter what). The fuzzer then decides when the parked operation should be executed next.

Partially completed operations. Syscalls arenât atomic, and a read racing a write can see the write partially applied. Suppose a program overwrites a few kilobytes of a file while another thread reads the same range. On ext4 the reader can see the old contents, the new contents, or a patchwork of old and new chunks. We let the fuzzer pick which of those the reader gets.

We implemented this in Amnesia by holding a write and splitting it into small chunks. Instead of applying them all, we let the fuzzer decide which chunks are applied immediately and which are held back. Combined with the out-of-order completion above, this means a read that arrives while the write is parked will likely be answered from the partially applied state, so it sees the same mix of old and new data that a real race could produce.

Similarly, reads can be held and split into pieces that are captured at different moments. For instance, a single read can return the start of the file from before a write and the end from after it. With several operations parked on the same file at once, the fuzzer picks the order they finish in. We ensure that every combination it tries is a legal interleaving that the kernel page cache or disk could have produced.

We built our FUSE filesystem to work hand in hand with the Antithesis fault injector and fuzzer. This lets us inject power failures, torn writes and disk I/O errors at moments our fuzzer considers âinterestingâ. It also means disk faults are controlled the same way as our other faults, so we get the benefits of swarm testing along the way.

Unlike our normal node kills fault, which could be interesting at any moment, with power failures we only need to sample one moment from one of the three categories of moments where a power failure can land: before the syscall, during it, or after it. Consider a single disk operation. Within âbeforeâ or âafterâ, the exact timing doesnât matter: if power failure is emulated anywhere in that window it will lead to the same outcome. The interesting states that are uncovered âduringâ an operation are relatively short, so these moments are rare especially in systems that touch the disk infrequently. By tying the fault to the disk operation itself, we let the fuzzer spend less energy finding these vulnerable states and more energy exploring from them.

Our disk fault injector helps the fuzzer by decreasing the uninteresting state space it has to explore. Instead of letting the fuzzer cut the power at arbitrary instants, it makes the decision on each syscall and injects the fault from inside the FUSE filesystem.

Each time the program is in the middle of a disk operation, there are three specific points where the injector may fire a power failure: before any of the operation has been applied to the internal cache, after part of it has been applied, and after all of it has been applied (but before the syscall returns). These three points line up with the three categories above: nothing applied, partly applied, or fully applied. When it does fire a power failure, the FUSE filesystem kills the container, deletes the internal cache, and makes sure any active syscalls are handled correctly. We call these correlated faults, because the timing of each power failure is tied to a specific disk operation.

Our work on disk fault injection has already earned its keep by uncovering a number of bugs in customer software. One open-source bug that we can share is in bbolt, the storage engine behind etcd. We injected all the disk faults in this post while testing the system, but the relevant ones for this particular bug are power failure and error injection.

The issue comes from bbolt committing a transaction in two steps that are each followed by an fsync. First it writes the new data pages, then it writes a single meta page that points at them.

We found a case where the data pages are written successfully, but the fsync of the meta page fails with an EIO. That causes etcd to exit, which is fine.

On restart, bbolt reads the meta page back through the kernel page cache, where the unpersisted meta page still exists, and wrongly treats that transaction as committed. It rebuilds its free page list from that meta page, so the next commits can reuse pages that the on-disk meta page still points to.

Once the cached meta page is evicted, through our emulation of memory pressure or power loss, what remains on disk is an old meta page pointing at overwritten pages. From then on bbolt panics at every open. The etcd nodeâs write-ahead log canât help rebuild the store, because the node never gets past opening it.

This bug could only be found by an I/O error followed by a power failure, which is exactly the kind of problem our disk fault injection finds.

Weâve covered a lot of ground: power failures, torn writes and torn sequences, disk I/O errors (including the one behind fsyncgate), and the latency faults that shake out concurrency bugs. All of these are available in our disk fault injector today, and the list keeps growing as customers tell us what keeps them up at night.

Our disk fault injector is customizable, so you donât have to turn everything on. You can start with the faults that worry you most â power loss for a storage engine, for example, or I/O errors â and add more over time.

If youâre an existing customer, ask your forward deployed engineer to deploy disk faults in your environment. If youâre not, and youâd like to see how your system holds up in nightmare mode, get in touch.

And if thereâs a disk failure youâve been bitten by that we havenât covered, weâd love to hear about it. The best faults in this post came from exactly those conversations :)

#9741. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:

We will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

#9740. Microsoft refreshes Copilot app search for users without an AI subscription

Meanwhile, Google's homepage demo leaves a familiar button out of the picture

Microsoft is updating search in its Microsoft 365 Copilot app for users without a Copilot license, with a toggle to restore the classic interface. Google, meanwhile, is giving AI searches more prominence on its homepage, where the familiar Search button is absent from a newly demonstrated layout.

Microsoft's change is rolling out now and will hit Deferred Release by mid-January 2027. It will impact users with a Microsoft 365 license who do not have a Copilot license and "provides modern search controls to help users find, refine, and navigate search results more easily."

It's enabled by default, which is a shame since administrators would likely prefer an opt-in rather than opt-out approach, and users can switch back to the "classic search experience" via a toggle on the search results page. Microsoft has not specified how long this toggle will remain available. Its separate Copilot Search experience had a fallback toggle scheduled for removal 60 days after general availability.

"With the updated search experience, users can continue to find files using keywords, use modern search controls to refine and navigate results, and search supported connected third-party content when their organization has configured connected sources," Microsoft said.

The results will still only display content to which users have permission. Microsoft advises administrators to brief users and help desks on the changed interface and the option to switch back.

Microsoft's search tweaks arrive as the future of the Google Search button on Google's desktop homepage looks uncertain.

In a post, Google VP of Product Robby Stein described a collapsible sidebar that lists users' recent AI conversations, pushing AI deeper into the search experience.  Stein called it "a much simpler way to pick up where you left off," and said it would help customers "easily find & jump back into your recent AI searches."

However, something else was obvious in Stein's post: the Google Search button was not present.

Stein explained in August that Google had performed a "small test on desktop to help people find new things they can do with Search." Part of that test was the removal of the Google Search button.

Users can still submit queries by pressing Enter. Stein said the test would have "no impact to how the core search works."

The sidebar rollout doesn't itself confirm the Search button's permanent retirement. For now, its absence from Stein's demonstration is another sign of which features Google wants users to notice. ®

#9739. Fund browser-grade certificate checking for every TLS client

Other software leaves users at risk while operators are responsible for timely remediation efforts across numerous platforms and application runtimes. upki brings platform-independent browser-grade protection to any TLS library, so everyone can benefit from better security and agility with minimal changes.

Help sponsor upki to make your TLS clients more secure, now and in the future.

Non-browser applications have historically relied on a slowly changing set of trust roots maintained by the operating system or platform vendors. These trust roots are often based on browser root programs, but lack the data that allow browsers to make fine-grained trust decisions: revocation data for end entities, intermediates and roots (like CRLite and OneCRL), distrust dates and Certificate Transparency policy.

The October 2026 eMudhra incident showed the cost. Browsers blocked the affected intermediates quickly, while other clients were unable to restrict only the affected intermediates. Instead, they had to wait for platform trust store updates to remove the parent root certificates and spent significant time and effort to mitigate the impact on their applications across different platforms and environments.

upki ships these signals as a compact local cache that's updated automatically, independently of applications, so every TLS stack on a machine can share one copy. Its checks only ever narrow what a client accepts: they never make it trust a certificate it would otherwise reject.

Sponsorships are annual and pay for maintainer time on the roadmap and on ongoing maintenance. We don't sell individual features; priorities are open for discussion with sponsors.

For more information, contact Dirkjan Ochtman.

Sponsors help set priorities through quarterly roadmap calls.

Clients outside the browser accept revoked end-entity certificates.

upki syncs compact CRLite filters several times a day and checks revocation offline.

When root programs distrust a CA or intermediate, other clients keep trusting it until a trust store package update arrives, as the eMudhra incident showed.

upki will ship OneCRL data, so distrust takes effect at the next cache update.

Post-quantum signatures would add kilobytes to every TLS handshake. Merkle Tree Certificates can bring down the costs, but clients need landmarks delivered ahead of time to minimize handshake overhead.

upki will distribute landmarks alongside its other data.

Clients that don't enforce Certificate Transparency accept certificates that were never publicly logged, so misissuance can go unnoticed. Clients also don't benefit from certificate transparency logs blocking compromised/distrusted roots from obtaining proof of inclusion.

upki will deliver and maintain an up-to-date log list and policy inputs, so applications don't have to configure logs manually.

Servers that send an incomplete certificate chain work in browsers but fail verification in other clients.

upki will ship the known intermediate certificates, so clients can complete the chain as browsers do, without expensive network fetching.

Root changes, including private PKI roots, reach machines through OS packages or configuration management, which can be slow and uneven across a fleet.

upki's sync mechanism could distribute root sets to every machine.

The checks only protect applications whose TLS stack uses upki.

upki could gain native support in OpenSSL upstream, GnuTLS, NSS or in language runtimes.

Every check depends on data that's refreshed several times a day, on upstream sources and formats that keep changing, and on prompt fixes when security issues come up.

Sponsorship pays for releases, security response, dependency updates, keeping the data pipeline running and in step with upstream changes, supporting distribution packagers and maintaining C2SP specifications.

upki lives in the rustls organization on GitHub and is dual-licensed under Apache-2.0 and MIT.

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Securing AI Agents in Production

Nov 23, 2026 3 min read

With agents now executing multi-step plans in live production environments, Walker argued that "a rogue AI agent is the same problem as a rogue human insider," one that acts with superhuman speed and persistence. Controls therefore need to work at machine speed, rather than relying on someone reviewing logs the next morning. She covered identity and credentials, boundary defence, subagent orchestration and policy-based containment.

Walker described giving an agent raw human credentials as the fastest path to production failure. The agent inherits the user's authority, so a prompt injection in a document can turn that access to an attacker's purposes. She recommended explicit principals for agents, the AI equivalent of service accounts, so each agent can be provisioned and logged separately without impersonating anyone.

Scoped OAuth tokens limit an agent's access in time and scope, but are immutable once issued. With credential attenuation, an orchestrator instead mints narrower tokens for its subagents, such as read-only access to logs, or read-only access to a repository between two commits when bisecting a broken build.

She pointed to Eclipse Biscuit, a token format whose holders can append restrictions, but cannot remove existing ones without invalidating its signature. It takes more work than reusing human authentication infrastructure, but suits services where teams control both ends.

For API keys, a proxy can give the agent a short-lived synthetic key and substitute the real one as traffic leaves, protecting it from prompt injection and exfiltration.

Walker cautioned that a virtual machine protects the host, not the resources an agent can reach: an agent with network access can still delete a database. Container sandboxes, ephemeral runtimes and sidecar proxies such as Envoy give finer control over file system and network access. But "a perfectly isolated compute sandbox is not useful," she said, so teams need policies that constrain what agents do with the services they call.

She also highlighted poisoned skills on public marketplaces that steal API keys and cryptocurrency wallets, citing Snyk research that found more than a third of publicly available skills had at least one security flaw.

Agents also cause harm by being wrong rather than malicious. Walker described an agent that read internal SRE documentation and invoked a break-glass process intended for emergencies, having decided it was the most expedient route. Monitoring caught it, but the lesson was that organisations must distinguish agents from the people they work for, because some processes depend on a human accepting risk. For the same reason, she described computer-use agents, which drive a mouse and keyboard, as in essence impersonation, while acknowledging they solve problems that machine protocols such as MCP cannot.

Asked in the question-and-answer session about tagging identities as agents, Walker said: "The biggest thing it gave us was auditability about some of these risk decisions." The distinction supports human-only rules, such as emergency access, and can help with agent-only rules, such as signed releases in regulated environments, although she noted that an agent flag alone is not enough for those.

In the Q&A, she also advised security teams not to simply say no, which pushes colleagues to work around controls, but to allow experimentation where mistakes are reversible and keep human review for irreversible actions such as wire transfers.
