#9677. Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:

<|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason,

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:

Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command:

You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID:

The repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model).

You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more.

llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K.

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:

The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API:

The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content.

The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs.

After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server:

This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request using the same Hub model ID:

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:

This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

#9676. ArcticRAT Cybercrime Gang Profiles Victim Finances With AI

The Android malware has expanded from focusing on cryptocurrency theft to full device control, and the attackers have added advanced analysis of stolen information.

Android cryptocurrency stealer ArcticRAT has evolved into a sophisticated remote access Trojan (RAT) capable of taking control of victim devices, harvesting sensitive information, and using AI to identify valuable financial data.

Researchers at Zimperium who are tracking the malware described it as representing a "dangerous escalation" in the mobile threat landscape. The newer versions, according to the vendor, give attackers the ability to interact with infected devices in real time, rather than relying purely on hardcoded actions.

The malware uses multiple techniques, including a "completely black, un-dismissible" screen overlay to conceal attacker activities from victims. Most significantly, the operators of ArcticRAT are now using large language model (LLM) services to automatically sift through stolen text messages and other data from infected device for financial information worth exploiting.

Related:APT29's Watering Holes Target Thousands of Mobile Users

"ArcticRAT uses AI to read through user information such as SMS messages to filter for financial information that could be used perform fraud," Nico Chiaraviglio, chief scientist at Zimperium, tells Dark Reading. "One particularly challenging technique is hidden remote control combined with a black-screen overlay. Attackers abuse legitimate Android features while making the device appear locked or powered off."

Defending against threats like ArcticRAT requires organizations to deploy AI-powered, on-device threat detection, enforce controls over application installation and permissions, and use runtime application protection to identify suspicious screen-sharing activity and malicious overlays, he adds.

Early versions of ArcticRAT targeted users of 11 specific cryptocurrency applications. Its primary purpose was to harvest sensitive information from infected Android devices that attackers could use to gain access to victims' cryptocurrency accounts.

In contrast, the newer versions that Zimperium is tracking pack considerably more capabilities. These include remote device control and surveillance, credential and keystroke theft, screen capture, live screen streaming, microphone monitoring, and the theft of SMS messages, contacts, and call logs. Another feature allows attackers to steal or change device lock-screen credentials, potentially locking victims out of their devices.

Since July, Zimperium analysts have identified 78 unique malware samples, 42 dropper samples, 36 payloads, and 21 IP addresses that the malware operators have been using for command-and-control communications. The researchers also identified 129 distinct commands that attackers can use to remotely control infected devices, steal information, monitor user activity, and manipulate device functions.

Related:Indonesia Hit by Android Banking App-Cloning Campaign

The operators of ArcticRAT 2.0 are using malvertising, smishing, and third-party forums to direct visitors to malicious websites in which the malware is embedded, "The primary attack vector," according to Zimperium, "relied on a landing page that convincingly impersonated Google Play to trick targets into downloading a malicious application." In some instances, the researchers observed the attackers using Amazon Web Services storage buckets to deliver the payload directly on Android devices.

Once installed, the latest version of ArcticRAT — like prior versions — abuses Android Accessibility Services permissions to connect with its command-and-control (C2) servers, giving attackers remote control over the device. The malware first collects information about the compromised device, including its location, battery status, screen state, Wi-Fi connectivity, and currently active applications.

It sends the information to the cyberattackers, who can then select which functions to activate based on the victim's device and installed applications. This can include actions as varied as capturing keystrokes, taking screenshots, recording screen activity, monitoring microphone audio and extracting sensitive information from messages and applications.

Related:ToxicPanda Banking Trojan Matures Into Enterprise Threat

One of the more significant additions to ArcticRAT is its use of artificial intelligence to analyze information stolen from compromised devices and identify data of potential financial value. Zimperium found the malware featuring an API connection to xAI's Grok model, which attackers can activate remotely to examine the victim's installed applications and identify banking, cryptocurrency, and trading platforms.

The new AI capabilities allow ArcticRAT to process stolen SMS messages, separate routine communications and promotional messages from information such as one-time authentication codes, account balance changes, and transaction notifications. It can even estimate a victim's financial standing before sending the information to its command-and-control infrastructure, according to Zimperium.

This allows attackers to automate much of the work involved in sorting through large volumes of stolen information and identifying potentially valuable financial intelligence, rather than having to manually examine the data themselves, according to the firm. "As mobile Trojan threats like ArcticRAT become increasingly sophisticated, conventional signature-based security layers are no longer sufficient to protect enterprise mobile endpoints."

ArcticRAT's transformation from a targeted cryptocurrency stealer into a sophisticated RAT is an example of how quickly mobile threats are evolving, with attackers using AI to make their malware more capable and dangerous. Analysts have noted how the trend underscores the need for users and organizations to stop treating their mobile devices as secondary security concerns and instead apply the same level of threat monitoring, access controls and security protections as they do to traditional endpoints.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9674. Beyond Linux: A Journey Through the Open Source Ecosystem

Notice: This site works best with JavaScript enabled, but all content is accessible without it. Skip to main content

What follows is the text of the talk I gave at Linux Day 2026 in Modena, lightly adapted for the blog. The talk was in Italian, in front of a Linux audience - which explains a few of the jokes.

Linux is one of the best-known players in the open source world, but it's not the only possible path. A journey through the BSDs, illumos and other alternative operating systems, to reflect on Open Source as an idea, a philosophy and a practice of sharing knowledge.

My name is Stefano Marinelli. I'm a sysadmin and consultant, and I run my own small company specialised in open source services and solutions. I like to call myself the "Barista" of the BSD Cafe and the illumos Cafe, online communities of people passionate about technology, open source and sharing. Today I'm not here just to talk about operating systems, but about freedom, sharing and knowledge. From free software to open source.

My first contact with the Free Software world was in 1996, when I wasn't even 17 yet. I saw a box set advertised in a magazine: "a whole operating system, for free", at a very low price. Something like 30,000 lire. Shortly before, I'd paid roughly ten times as much for the Windows 95 upgrade edition. Dismissive and without a shred of trust, I decided to order it and give it a go. I mean: who would ever write something like that... and release the source code? But six CDs for 30,000 lire... let's try. Worst case, it'll be an experience.

It was love at first shell. That terminal opened up a whole universe, and to what I already knew (commercial licences, freeware, shareware) I added the concept of Free Software. But I didn't have enough hardware to run two operating systems, so I reinstalled Windows and put it all off. Still, I started thinking. Reflecting. Studying. In 1997 I got a new PC and started using Linux - or, as I was careful to say, GNU/Linux - for everything. Except games. For those, a small Windows partition survived, though not for long.

In 1998 I enrolled in Computer Science at the University of Bologna. Even back then, it was a faculty strongly oriented towards free software. Linux in the labs. I was one of the few who, in the first year, already knew what Free Software was (not free as in price, but...freedom!) and how to use the Linux workstations. That gave me a big advantage, especially from the second year onwards. Renzo Davoli was already pushing hard in that direction. I decided that would be my path. And so it was, and I started pushing too. Windows wasn't the "enemy" to me. The imposition was. Personally, I respect rules, but not impositions. Some people followed me, others watched from a distance. I didn't care. I was widening my horizons.

In the early 2000s I also discovered the BSDs. And I convinced my parents that I needed a laser printer for "university material". In reality, I wanted to print the excellent BSD documentation. Maybe not university material, but the printed FreeBSD Handbook probably served me better than half of the theory exams I took back then. Thanks, mom and dad!

Free Software was born out of a change. In those days, code circulated freely among people. Depending on their needs, they exchanged source code, modified it and shared it again. But at some point this began to change. There's an anecdote that, while not exhaustive, gives the idea: the printer Richard Stallman was using kept jamming, and nobody got notified. He wanted to modify the software so that he'd get a notification, as he'd done with the previous printer. Back then it was common practice, but this time he was refused. "I can't share the source code. It's under NDA." In other words, he had lost control over what he was using. He even wanted to improve the program, and instead he got a refusal.

The rest is history. At least until a few years ago.

Because thirty years ago we fought for Free Software to be taken seriously. When I started working, I was almost laughed at. "That's toy stuff you use at university. The real world uses something else." "Why don't you just use Windows? Everything's easier." And yet, the toys often worked better than the expensive proprietary solutions. Or at least just as well, at a fraction of the cost. "Let's try. Don't pay me until you're satisfied." They smiled, incredulous. Then they paid, happily. We could prove there was an alternative. Free, with no artificial locks. Something that anyone - even the broke but eager student - could study and set up. Technology, that kind of "enterprise" technology, was truly within everyone's reach. There was no need to buy expensive products, or recurring certifications just to have the "right" to work on them. You study, you apply yourself, nobody can stop you. I attended Linux Days. I spoke at Linux Days. For example, here I am, in Linux Day 2004.

We won that battle. We won that war. Linux - chaotic Linux, built by countless external contributors, made of different and varied distributions - has reached everywhere. Open Source is everywhere. But something happened - something beautiful, but terrible: precisely because it reached everywhere, something changed in the spirit. "Too big to fail". And so the big players arrived. Today, Linux development is driven by corporate money: companies like Microsoft (the same Microsoft that once considered Linux its sworn enemy - or Red Hat itself) and other big tech players. In itself, this has been a good thing. In practice, though, it means that they steer its development, even if indirectly. Year after year, it has started to take the shape of a different kind of product. Is the user still at the centre, or is it more code to make Azure run better? Sure, it's Open Source, it's free. But it's increasingly close to the needs of the big companies funding its development and, at times, further from the ordinary user. That's not necessarily bad: many of these investments have given us extraordinary technologies.

But I wonder whether, in the process, we're losing something. Not so much in the code as in the mindset. If not in the kernel, then in the community around it.

Back then, precisely because we were frustrated by "It only works on Windows", we were careful to write portable software. I'll say one word, without going into too much detail: POSIX. Once a mantra: POSIX compliant. A set of standards defining common interfaces between operating systems, so you can write programs that, with few or even no changes, run on different Unix and Unix-like systems. Today, in the communities around Linux, you hear more and more often that POSIX is "outdated". When I send a patch to make a specific tool work on FreeBSD, for example, I often read comments like: "Why don't you just use Linux?". And that dÃ©jÃ  vu sends a shiver down my spine: is the community I loved so much turning into a copy, albeit a better one, of its worst enemy?

But careful: I'm not here to speak ill of Linux. That would be absurd. I mean: coming to Linux Day to trash Linux? It's an extraordinary operating system, and I owe it a great deal.

I'm here to remind you that Linux isn't the only way to understand free software. And that a project being less well known doesn't make it less interesting, less valid or less worthy of attention. Because if freedom of choice is truly a value, we must be ready to defend it even when someone chooses something different from what we choose.

So let's see what lies beyond Linux. Because monoculture is a problem, in Open Source too.

Because free software is...free. And we must be free too. Free to choose, to consider alternatives. To contribute, if we want to. To understand which solution best fits our problem. We don't have to pick a single solution "because everyone does". We don't have to turn one monopoly into another. Linux is great. It helps put bread on my table, so I'm a fan. But there are alternatives, other solutions, that can have their advantages. And that's why I want to talk to you about the BSDs and illumos.

BSD stands for Berkeley Software Distribution. And the first curious thing is that its story begins before Linux even existed. We're in the late Seventies. At the University of California, Berkeley, some researchers are working on UNIX, the operating system developed at AT&T's Bell Labs. They don't just use it. They modify it, improve it, write new programs and share that work with other universities.

Remind you of something? We've just been talking about Stallman and the culture of sharing.

BSD was born in exactly that world. So it was born on solid, stable, reliable foundations. Studied by experts, not as a game. BSD was an operating system directly related to Unix. It was a complete and stable system, but it wasn't yet available for "home" systems, the i386 family. Born well before Linux. A curiosity: Linus Torvalds himself, in a 1993 interview, said: "If 386BSD had been available when I started on Linux, Linux would probably never had happened.". Yes, you heard that right. Linus Torvalds said it. And we're at a Linux Day!

Then something happened: BSD arrived on the i386, and Unix System Laboratories, controlled by AT&T, started a rather insidious legal dispute: there's our code in BSD and you have no right to use, modify or share it. The University of California was dragged into it too. This was a real blocker for many. Companies were afraid to adopt an operating system with a lawsuit like that in progress. The matter dragged on until 1994, when a settlement was reached and 4.4BSD-Lite was released, with a freely redistributable and legally cleared base.

Meanwhile, Linux was growing, attracting developers, winning users. It didn't have that particular legal uncertainty. I'm not saying Linux succeeded only because of this. That would be unfair to Torvalds and to the thousands of people who contributed to its development.

But it's interesting to think that the history of computing as we know it could have taken a different path. And it's also interesting that, despite these difficulties, BSD didn't disappear. Quite the opposite.

From that story came some of the operating systems I want to talk about today. Systems that took different paths and that are still developed, used and improved. Different operating systems - careful, not distributions of the same operating system! - each unique in its own way. Let's start with FreeBSD.

FreeBSD is probably the most general-purpose BSD. It's a complete operating system, designed to offer stability, performance and a certain consistency in administration. And here's a first difference from Linux I'd like to highlight. In the BSDs, the kernel and the userland, the base tools of the operating system, are developed and maintained within the same project. That doesn't mean Linux works worse. It means the development model is different.

And there's a philosophy I really appreciate: evolution, not revolution. It doesn't mean standing still. It means trying to improve without necessarily turning upside down what already works.

Let's talk about some technologies. ZFS, for example. An advanced filesystem, with snapshots, data integrity, replication and many other features. FreeBSD integrates it directly into the system and also lets you use Boot Environments: I can upgrade the system and, if something goes wrong, go back to the previous environment.

Then we have jails. FreeBSD has had a technology for isolating processes, resources and application environments since 2000. Long before Docker arrived. Jails aren't Docker, and I'm not saying they're the same thing. But they let you isolate applications and services simply, with low overhead, using the operating system's own features directly. A bit like LXC on Linux.

For virtualisation we have bhyve, which lets you run virtual machines, including other operating systems. And bhyve is lighter and, often, faster than KVM on Linux. [LINK: my bhyve articles]

But FreeBSD isn't just a system for enthusiasts. Netflix uses it to deliver video content. PlayStation consoles have a FreeBSD-derived base. macOS and iOS also include code from the BSD world. OPNsense and pfSense, two well-known firewall solutions, are based on FreeBSD. In short, we're not talking about a university toy. Remind you of something?

Personally, I've been using FreeBSD for many years, in production too. And it has often let me solve problems simply, while staying in control of what's happening. I've seen cases where, on the same hardware and with the same workload, FreeBSD handled I/O pressure better, with even very significant reductions in execution time. If you're curious, there are several articles about it here on IT Notes. That doesn't mean FreeBSD is always faster than Linux. That would be nonsense. It means there are situations where it can be the better choice.

And for me, this is the point: I solve problems. I don't have to defend an operating system. I have to pick the right tool.

Then there's OpenBSD. OpenBSD was born in 1995 as a fork of NetBSD and is probably one of the most interesting systems when we talk about security and code correctness.

Its philosophy is fairly simple: less complexity, fewer chances for mistakes. The code is continuously reviewed, cleaned up, simplified. Features aren't added just because they might be interesting. Every choice has to make sense within the project. Because the more complex code becomes, the harder it is to maintain, audit and verify.

OpenBSD has also developed some very interesting security mechanisms, like pledge() and unveil(), which let you restrict the operations a program can perform and the parts of the filesystem it can access.

And then there's OpenSSH. Yes, the very OpenSSH you probably use every day to manage your servers. It was born, and is developed, within the OpenBSD project.

But there's another feature I love: the documentation. In the OpenBSD world, insufficient or wrong documentation is considered a bug. The man pages are often enough to understand how to use and configure the system, without hunting for guides of dubious quality scattered across the Internet. And believe me, when you manage dozens or hundreds of systems, knowing where to find correct and consistent information is a huge advantage.

OpenBSD doesn't try to please everyone. The developers follow their own priorities, even when that means giving up something other systems offer. Can it be frustrating? Certainly. But it also offers a great advantage: consistency, predictability and a clear design direction.

For firewalls, routers and systems where security is particularly important, it's an alternative always worth considering.

NetBSD, on the other hand, has a wonderful motto. "Of course it runs NetBSD!" And that already says a lot about its philosophy.

NetBSD puts a huge emphasis on portability, correctness of implementation and the ability to run on very different hardware architectures. Not just modern x86 or ARM computers. We're also talking about machines decades old, architectures many consider long forgotten. And careful: it's not just a matter of computing nostalgia.

Keeping an operating system working on such different platforms forces you to write code with great attention to portability, avoiding needless dependencies on a specific architecture.

Remember when, a moment ago, I was talking about POSIX and portability as a value? Well, NetBSD is one of the best examples of that philosophy. Because a system that can run on very different hardware must necessarily care about how correct, clean and portable its code is. And that has positive consequences on the more common platforms too.

There's another aspect I appreciate: continuity. We don't always need the latest novelty, the latest feature, the latest framework. Some devices and applications simply need to keep working, maybe for many years. Think of embedded systems, small computers, hardware that isn't replaced every two years. In these contexts, knowing there's a project that considers portability and support for different architectures a fundamental part of its identity is reassuring.

It's a different philosophy from FreeBSD's and from OpenBSD's. And that's absolutely fine.

NetBSD has also taken a clear stance on AI-generated code: it can't be committed without prior written approval, because it's considered potentially "tainted" - both in form and in licence. And in today's extremely polarised world, that's a sigh of relief for anyone who wants to use and develop an operating system without the pressure of always having to do more, add more features and more code.

There's also DragonFlyBSD, born in 2003 as a fork of FreeBSD, which followed other design choices, especially regarding the kernel and system management. We don't have time to go into everything, but I want to stress one thing. These systems have common origins and share part of their history, but they don't necessarily have the same goals.

FreeBSD is a general-purpose system, also oriented towards performance and production environments. It's stable and secure. On the desktop it might not support all the hardware Linux does, although they're working on it. But on servers it could be one of the best alternatives to Linux.

OpenBSD favours security, simplicity and code correctness. NetBSD focuses heavily on portability and on supporting different hardware. DragonFlyBSD has experimented with other architectural solutions. And yet, they all belong to the big BSD family.

There's no need for one to win over the others. It's not a battle. There's nothing to sell here. It's freedom. It's diversity. And that diversity is a strength.

If there's one thing I've learnt over all these years, it's exactly this: an operating system shouldn't be a religion. In my daily life, I solve problems. And to solve them, I need to be able to evaluate the alternatives.

Because stability, for example, isn't just a system's ability not to crash. It's also being able to update it without surprises, to understand how it works, to know what happens when something goes wrong. Observability is fundamental, and being able to have it without weaving together fifty Docker containers can sometimes make the difference between ten minutes of work and two hours.

We don't always need to reinvent everything. What's new isn't always better. And the solution chosen by the majority isn't always the best fit for our problem. Often, it's exactly the opposite.

But our journey doesn't end with the BSDs.

There's another family of operating systems that descends from a different UNIX history. A history that runs through Sun Microsystems, Solaris and OpenSolaris. And that leads us to illumos.

Now someone might ask: weren't you talking about the BSDs? Yes, but the talk is called Beyond Linux, not Only BSD!

illumos isn't a BSD. It descends from another branch of the big UNIX family. The Solaris one, developed by Sun Microsystems. Sun. Anyone remember it? SPARC workstations, servers, Solaris, Java. In the Nineties and the 2000s it was one of the biggest names in professional computing.

And Solaris was a very interesting operating system. Designed for serious machines, serious workloads, situations where a problem could cost a lot. In Bologna, when I was a student, there were some Solaris machines in the UnderLab. I looked at them sideways. To me they were "non-Linux". So I didn't like them.

In 2005 Sun did something significant: it started publishing the Solaris source code through the OpenSolaris project. Imagine: a commercial UNIX system, with years of development behind it, advanced technologies and long experience in enterprise environments, opening up to the community. It wasn't the first free software to be used in companies, of course. But it was another way of doing things. Another model.

And then, in 2010, Oracle acquired Sun. And here things changed. Oracle decided to stop the open development of OpenSolaris and stopped publishing new code updates.

Because the code that had already been released under an open source licence remained available. Oracle could decide not to publish its developments any more, but it couldn't take back the freedoms already granted on that code. And that's how illumos was born. A group of developers decided to carry on the work, starting from the open OpenSolaris base.

Think about it for a moment. A company acquires another company, changes strategy and stops the public development of an operating system. But that system doesn't die. Because the code exists, the skills exist, and there are people willing to keep working on it.

Remind you of something? We began this talk with Stallman and a printer whose code couldn't be shared. Thirty years later, the very possibility of sharing and modifying code allows a whole family of operating systems to keep existing.

This, for me, is one of the most beautiful aspects of free software.

But let's get back to the technology. Because illumos isn't just a nice story.

From Solaris, illumos inherited some extremely interesting technologies. You already know one: ZFS. ZFS was born at Sun. It's a filesystem, but also a volume manager. It lets you manage storage, snapshots, data replication, integrity checks and much more.

I use ZFS practically everywhere I can. On FreeBSD, on illumos, on NetBSD and on Linux too. And that's already an example of how a good technology can cross different operating systems.

Then we have DTrace. DTrace lets you observe what's happening inside a system, even while it's running. We can analyse kernel calls, processes, performance, behaviours that would otherwise be hard to understand. For a sysadmin, it's an extraordinary tool. Because when a client tells you "the server is slow", the problem isn't knowing it's slow. They already know that. The problem is understanding why.

Then there are Zones. An isolation system that lets you run separate environments sharing the same kernel. Remember FreeBSD's jails? Well, zones were inspired by FreeBSD's jails. The concept is similar, although the implementations and some features differ.

And then Crossbow, for network virtualisation. SMF, for managing services and their dependencies. In short, we're talking about a system with important technologies, born to tackle concrete problems. Not an experiment cobbled together in someone's spare time. And careful, I'm not saying these technologies are necessarily better than those available on Linux or the BSDs. I'm saying they're different, they have their own history and, in certain contexts, they can be particularly useful.

Like Linux, illumos is the base of several distributions, each with different features and goals.

SmartOS, for example, is focused on virtualisation. It has an interesting peculiarity: the operating system is loaded into RAM, from USB or from the network (or even from the local disk, but then it runs read-only), leaving the disks to the virtual machines and the data, managed with ZFS. It supports native Zones, LX zones to run Linux applications, and virtual machines via KVM and bhyve. Yes, the very bhyve we've already met talking about FreeBSD! Personally, I'm using and experimenting with it a lot. It's not all roses, but I really like some of its solutions. And bhyve on illumos even has a few gems that haven't been brought back to FreeBSD. Open Source and collaboration between projects, at their best!

OmniOS takes a more traditional road. It's an operating system designed mainly for servers, with particular attention to stability, updates and long-term continuity. It offers stable releases and long-term support versions. You install it, configure your services and use it. Without necessarily having to reinvent everything at every update.

OpenIndiana is perhaps the closest to the classic idea of a general-purpose UNIX distribution. It can be used on servers, but also as a desktop system, with a full graphical environment. For anyone who'd like to try a Solaris-derived system on their own computer, it could be an interesting starting point.

And then there's Tribblix, a rather special project. Created by Peter Tribble, it combines an almost nostalgic, traditional UNIX feel with modern components. It has its own package management system and a modular approach through overlays, which let you install groups of software. A small, independent system with a very precise personality.

Four distributions sharing a technological base, but interpreting it in different ways. Remind you of something? Linux... And that's exactly the point. There's no single way to build an operating system. There's no single development philosophy.

And none of them needs to prevail over the others. What matters is that they keep existing, evolving and offering alternatives. Because, in the end, freedom of choice only has value if we really have something to choose from.

Because there's a whole UNIX tradition that isn't Linux and isn't BSD. Because some technologies now considered fundamental in modern computing were born right there. And, still today, they're stable and reliable. They're refined and polished without being "rewritten" or replaced every five years because there's a new fashion. Because we can use systems that followed different paths, with different architectures and design choices.

But above all, because illumos is also a practical demonstration of the value of free software. Sun opened the code. Oracle decided to stop that open development. The community was able to carry on.

It wasn't easy, and it doesn't mean every open source project can automatically survive the disappearance of whoever was funding it. You need developers, resources, skills. You need someone willing to take care of it. Available code is a necessary condition, but on its own it isn't enough.

And this brings us to a point that, for me, is fundamental. Free software isn't just code. It's also the people who choose to develop it, maintain it, document it and share it.

That's why, alongside the BSD Cafe, I also wanted to create the illumos Cafe. To offer a space to meet, discuss and share experiences about technologies that maybe don't make the front pages of tech sites every day.

Because we don't all have to use the same operating system. We don't even all have to agree. But we can learn something from each other. And maybe discover a solution to a problem we didn't even know we could tackle differently.

Careful, though. I'm not saying the BSD or illumos communities are better than the Linux ones. In our world too there's fundamentalism, prejudice, and people who consider their own choice the only possible one. And that's a problem too. Because it makes no sense to defend software freedom and then look down on someone who decides to use a system different from ours.

We don't all have to agree. In fact, it would be terribly boring. We must be able to disagree, compare ideas, learn something and keep respecting each other - even in disagreement - while building something constructive. What matters, in the end, is being able to choose. And that's true freedom.

More than twenty years ago, at Linux Days, I talked about how Linux could replace Windows in many areas, both on the desktop and on servers. That it was a valid alternative. Today I'm here to tell you not to let yourselves be chained by habit. Linux/Docker/Kubernetes is an exceptional combination, but not the only one. It would be serious if it were, because we'd have lost our freedom. The freedom to publish an Open Source project as a tarball of source code instead of putting it "on GitHub" or similar.

Open source is not about doing things the approved way. It is about giving people the freedom to do things another way.

Open Source and Closed Minds never get along.

Compare static web hosting performance on an Intel N150 using the same nginx.conf across FreeBSD jails, SmartOS zones, NetBSD, OpenBSD and Linux, focusing on HTTP vs HTTPS and TLS CPU usage.

The slides, the video, and the text behind my presentation at EuroBSDCon 2024 and BSDCan 2025 - Why and how we're migrating many of our servers from Linux to the BSDs.

#9673. Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

#9672. As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

It's hard to detect whether someone is using artificial intelligence to cheat on IT certification exams, but new tools and processes are emerging to boost trust.

Certifications play a critical role in keeping up with the latest industry trends and in establishing expertise, but artificial intelligence (AI) is muddying the verification process and making it difficult for organizations to know whether the person they hired can actually do what their certifications say they can.

Available certification options abound, from entry-level cloud and cybersecurity knowledge to specific Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services technologies. In some industries, such as government, banking, and financial services, certified IT departments are required to stay current with compliance regulations.

But exam administrators face a growing list of risks to monitor — including Meta Glasses, AI browsers, and deepfakes — which cast doubt on the legitimacy of scores. As a result, the industry is shifting toward more in-person testing and stricter fraud-detection protocols.

Related:Behind the Alias: How One Researcher Unmasked a Decade of Ransomware Actors

Cheating has existed for as long as testing has. But AI has significantly changed the testing game for IT certifications, says Marielle Carlos, data forensics scientist at Caveon, which offers test security technologies and services to help organizations design and administer tests.

Methods such as harvesting pre-knowledge, plagiarism, and collusion proxy testing have evolved as people increasingly use AI as an unauthorized aid, she says. Troublingly, the cheating problem is still in its infancy. Caveon had identified six distinct ways people could cheat on these exams, but with AI blurring the lines between these tidy buckets, it's hard to tell whether an AI agent is gathering test questions in advance or helping during the test itself. To capture emerging anomalies that seem likely related to AI, Carlos created a seventh "unknown" tag in the company's threat-tracking taxonomy, she says.

"It makes it hard to know if your exam is measuring actual competence or if it's measuring someone's ability to use AI to answer the question," Carlos tells Dark Reading. "It really challenges the usefulness of that exam."

Carlos spends her day interpreting test results to help programs decide whether anomalies warrant additional attention or professional review. Over the past two years, she has seen how AI has changed the way certification programs monitor metrics to assess cheating. Whereas once it was enough to look at speed and score separately to flag a case for review, administrators are now forced to take numerous variables into account since AI can combine multiple cheating tactics.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

During her research, Carlos noted a "huge boom of people" who are testing fast and receiving high scores. There is no concrete data indicating it's entirely due to AI, but enough organizational interest and concern exists that Carlos says she and her team plan to look into it further.

But uncertainty hasn't stopped other organizations from taking action. Widespread irregularities in exam results and verified cheating attempts during ISC2's online proctoring pilot exams led the nonprofit to shift to in-person testing, says Casey Marks, ISC2's chief operating officer. The consortium also implemented "the most stringent security protocols available to analyze each result and detect irregularities," including biometric and identity verification.

The testing environment mirrors the most stringent conditions used by licensed professionals, such as doctors, to provide the highest level of security available in the industry, Marks says. Regarding AI use, the fact that ISC2 offers all exams exclusively through test centers ensures that outside resources or technology are not available during exam administration, he adds.

"The candidate, the employer, and every other professional holding that credential depend on the credibility of the process," Marks tells Dark Reading.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

Regardless of AI introducing new risks, certifications remain one of the most universal ways for employers to validate a candidate's necessary knowledge and skills when making hiring or promotion decisions, Marks adds.

Carlos agrees but urges conversations around protecting score validity across the entire process. A layered approach is crucial because even though tools can indicate possible AI use, "it's hard to pinpoint exactly," she says. "That includes secure exam design, control during administration, analysis of results, and a clear process for responding to your security concerns."

Carlos cites an experiment by Sarah Toton, director of data forensics at Caveon, that compared AI and human test-taking and found "distinct differences" in response timing. The research focused on test results and response patterns.

"When someone uses AI, they're often six to 48 times faster compared to an individual test taker," she explains. "That said, AI can get some things wrong sometimes, particularly the questions that involve some realm of human judgment."

It's ironic, but the same technology that enables people to cheat on exams is also becoming one of the most in-demand certifications employers rely on to validate real skills. Many certifications, like ISC2's Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), continue to evolve to address the impact of AI on security best practices, Marks says. That's in addition to new AI-specific security certifications entering the market. The Computing Technology Industry Association launched SecAI+ earlier this year to help organizations secure, govern, and responsibly integrate AI into their cybersecurity operations.

"As certifications evolve, especially with AI now playing a key role in so many facets of our work, the value of certifications for employers is increasing," Marks says.

The pressure remains on certification administrators to keep up.

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

#9671. Beyls: Wrapping up LLVM's relicensing effort

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...]

Today, more than 99.5% of all lines of code ever contributed to LLVM are either covered by the new license, too small for copyright to apply, or no longer in the repository.

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

The LLVM exception to Apache-2 Posted Nov 21, 2026 13:13 UTC (Sat) by coriordan (guest, #7544) [Link] For anyone who doesn't know (like me until 5 minutes ago): The LLVM exception: https://merlijn.sebrechts.be/blog/what-is-the-apache-2-ll... It says two things. (Based on my quick read; corrections welcome) 1. That Apache-2 licensed compilers (which insert some compiler code into the executables they create) don't create Apache-2 obligations for the programs they create. 2. It fixes incompatibility with GPLv2 by saying that, for a combined work of Apache-2 plus GPLv2 code, if an authority decides that any clause of Apache-2 is incompatible with GPLv2 then that clause of Apache-2 doesn't apply. (Which I guess they decided is fine because the places where there could be conflicts, such as patents, using the GPLv2 version isn't enough of a problem to be worth incompatibility.) So, the LLVM exception looks like a pretty good instrument.

InfoQ Homepage News CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve

Nov 24, 2026 3 min read

Virtual machines (VMs) continue to account for a substantial share of cloud-native production infrastructure, despite the widespread adoption of containers and Kubernetes. New research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required.

The report surveyed 492 cloud-native practitioners and technology leaders in September 2026. Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 34% identified AI and agentic workloads as a contributing factor. The findings suggest that rather than replacing virtual machines with containers, organisations are increasingly combining the two to accommodate different application and security requirements.

The research challenges the assumption that cloud-native adoption necessarily means moving away from virtual machines. While containers provide portability and efficient application packaging, VMs continue to offer isolation and support for workloads that depend on dedicated operating systems or established virtualisation environments.

The survey found that 51% of respondents run at least half of their production applications on VMs. This rises to an average of 64% in organisations with more than 10,000 employees, compared with 45% among organisations with fewer than 500 employees.

Furthermore, 71% of respondents who provided both current and expected workload figures anticipate their VM share remaining within the same range over the next year. This points towards continued coexistence rather than a wholesale migration to one deployment model.

One of the more significant findings concerns the relationship between AI adoption and infrastructure security.

AI agents increasingly generate and execute code, interact with tools, and access external systems. This creates new risks when generated code is executed in environments containing sensitive data or shared infrastructure.

Virtual machines offer a stronger isolation boundary than conventional containers, which share the host operating system kernel. The report identifies hardware-level VM isolation, containers running inside VMs, and MicroVM sandboxing as approaches organisations are using to contain AI workloads.

Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 47% cited security and isolation as a contributing factor, while 34% specifically identified AI and agentic workloads.

The survey also points to growing interest in stronger isolation technologies. MicroVM sandboxing adoption is expected to increase from 20% current use to 30% planned use, while confidential computing is expected to grow from 12% to 26%. These figures represent reported intentions rather than confirmed deployments.

Some 61% of respondents described their VM and container administration teams as collaborative or fully integrated, suggesting that managing different workload types is increasingly becoming a shared platform engineering responsibility.

Kubernetes is also beginning to play a role in virtual machine management. Among respondents using VMs, 8% reported using KubeVirt, the CNCF project that allows virtual machines to be managed through Kubernetes resources and APIs.

This brings VM lifecycle management into existing Kubernetes operational practices without requiring applications to abandon their virtualised environments.

The findings reinforce a shift in how cloud-native infrastructure is evolving. Kubernetes and containers remain important, but they are not necessarily the right execution model for every workload.

Technologies such as KubeVirt and Kata Containers show how virtualisation can integrate with container orchestration, while MicroVMs provide lightweight environments to isolate short-lived or potentially untrusted workloads.

For platform engineering teams, the research highlights the need to accommodate different execution environments without fragmenting operational practices. AI adds another dimension, making isolation, resource utilisation and workload security increasingly important infrastructure considerations.

The survey was sponsored by CNCF and Broadcom, and its results should be read as reported industry perspectives rather than a complete census of cloud-native deployments. Nevertheless, its findings provide a useful indication of where infrastructure priorities are moving.
