#9589. AI Programming Tutor: How to Use AI to Learn Programming Faster

Artificial intelligence is changing the software development process. AI-powered coding assistants can generate functions, refactor existing code, write unit tests, explain unfamiliar repositories, and suggest solutions to complex programming problems. Some tools can even generate complete application components from natural-language instructions.

These capabilities have changed how developers approach implementation. Instead of writing every line manually, engineers can delegate repetitive coding tasks, explore alternative implementations, and accelerate development workflows.

However, generating syntactically correct code is not equivalent to engineering a reliable software system.

Software development requires much more than producing code that executes successfully. Developers must understand algorithmic complexity, memory management, data structures, concurrency, type systems, exception handling, security boundaries, and architectural dependencies. They must also evaluate whether an implementation satisfies functional and non-functional requirements.

An AI-generated solution may pass a basic execution test while containing race conditions, inefficient algorithms, incorrect assumptions, or security vulnerabilities.

This creates an important distinction between using AI to generate code and possessing the programming knowledge required to evaluate that code.

AI should improve the efficiency of software engineering, but it should not replace the technical understanding that makes software development possible.

AI coding assistants are particularly effective at generating familiar programming patterns. They can produce REST API endpoints, database queries, utility functions, validation logic, and common data-processing operations.

Consider a Python function that determines whether a list contains duplicate values.

This implementation is concise and generally efficient.

However, evaluating it properly requires understanding several technical considerations:

For a list containing n elements, the expected time complexity is O(n), with O(n) additional space complexity.

This implementation can terminate early when it encounters a duplicate.

The distinction becomes important when working with large datasets or when duplicate values are common near the beginning of an input sequence.

A developer who understands algorithmic complexity can evaluate these alternatives based on workload characteristics. A developer who simply accepts generated code may overlook the operational implications.

For further technical reference, the Python implementation's time complexity documentation explains the average-case and worst-case behavior of common data structure operations.

The objective of AI-assisted programming should therefore extend beyond code generation to include technical evaluation and informed decision-making.

One of the most important responsibilities of a software engineer is selecting algorithms that perform efficiently under realistic workloads.

AI can generate an algorithm that produces the correct output without necessarily selecting the most appropriate computational approach.

Consider the problem of finding two numbers in an array whose sum equals a target value.

A straightforward implementation uses nested loops:

This implementation has O(n²) time complexity because it potentially examines every pair of elements.

For a small input, the performance may be acceptable. For a large input, the number of comparisons increases rapidly.

A hash-based implementation provides a more efficient expected-time solution:

The expected time complexity is O(n), with O(n) additional space complexity.

The algorithm stores previously encountered values in a dictionary and checks whether the required complement already exists.

This example demonstrates why understanding data structures matters.

An AI assistant may generate both implementations, but a developer must understand:

For production systems, these considerations become increasingly important as input sizes and request volumes grow.

Type annotations improve code readability and help static analysis tools detect certain classes of programming errors.

However, Python type annotations are not automatically enforced at runtime.

Consider an application that processes customer transactions:

The function assumes that every transaction contains a valid decimal amount.

However, external API responses, CSV files, and database records may contain malformed data.

The amount is a string rather than a Decimal instance.

A type annotation alone does not guarantee that incoming data satisfies the declared structure.

A more robust implementation validates external data before processing it:

This example introduces several important engineering principles:

Developers can use tools such as mypy to perform static type checking and identify inconsistencies before execution. Python's decimal module documentation also explains decimal arithmetic and its use cases.

AI-generated code may provide the initial implementation, but developers must determine whether the implementation respects the application's data contracts and business rules.

Debugging is one of the clearest examples of why programming knowledge cannot be reduced to code generation.

Consider an asynchronous Python application that processes multiple requests.

A developer might encounter unexpected behavior because multiple coroutines modify shared state.

However, the actual result can be lower because multiple coroutines may read the same value before updating it.

The problem is a race condition caused by non-atomic read-modify-write operations.

An AI assistant may identify the issue, but understanding asynchronous execution makes it possible to explain why it occurs.

One solution is to protect the shared state using an asynchronous lock:

The lock ensures that only one coroutine at a time executes the critical section.

This example also highlights an important distinction: asynchronous execution does not automatically provide parallel execution, and shared mutable state still requires appropriate synchronization.

Developers must understand event loops, coroutine scheduling, synchronization primitives, and execution boundaries to diagnose these problems correctly.

The official Python asyncio synchronization documentation explains how locks and other synchronization primitives work.

AI can suggest a correction, but the engineer must verify whether the correction is appropriate for the application's concurrency model.

A program executing without an exception does not establish that it is correct.

Reliable software requires systematic testing across normal inputs, boundary conditions, invalid data, and unexpected execution paths.

Consider the earlier duplicate-detection function.

A developer can write unit tests using pytest:

These tests cover several representative input conditions.

The pytest parametrization documentation explains how developers can execute the same test against multiple input and expected-output combinations.

Property-based testing checks general properties across many generated inputs rather than relying exclusively on manually selected examples.

This test generates different integer lists and verifies that the function behaves consistently with the expected set-based definition.

Property-based testing can expose edge cases that developers may not think to include in conventional test cases.

The Hypothesis documentation provides additional examples of generated test data, strategies, and property-based testing techniques.

Unit tests validate individual components, but they cannot establish that all system components work together correctly.

Integration testing should examine interactions involving:

AI-generated code should also be evaluated against realistic workloads.

For example, a developer might benchmark two implementations using Python's timeit module:

Both implementations have different performance characteristics depending on the input distribution.

The early-exit implementation can be advantageous when duplicates occur early. Set conversion can be preferable when the entire collection must be examined and the implementation's simplicity is valuable.

The correct choice should be based on actual requirements and measured performance rather than assumptions.

Python's timeit documentation provides guidance on measuring execution time for small code segments.

AI-generated code can introduce security vulnerabilities when developers accept implementations without reviewing their behavior.

Consider an application that constructs a database query using user input:

This approach is vulnerable to SQL injection because user-controlled input becomes part of the SQL statement.

A safer implementation uses parameterized queries:

The database driver handles the parameter separately from the SQL statement.

This prevents user input from being interpreted as executable SQL syntax in this query.

The OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet explains why parameterized queries are a preferred defense and why manually constructing SQL statements with untrusted input is dangerous.

An AI assistant may generate code that appears functionally correct but does not account for the application's threat model.

Security engineering requires developers to understand how data moves through a system, where trust boundaries exist, and how attackers might exploit unexpected behavior.

The most effective approach is to use AI as an engineering assistant while maintaining responsibility for technical decisions.

A structured workflow can help achieve this.

Before generating code, establish the expected behavior, input constraints, output format, performance requirements, and failure conditions.

For example, instead of asking AI to create a file-processing function, specify:

Clear requirements reduce ambiguity and make generated implementations easier to evaluate.

AI can assist with boilerplate code, repetitive transformations, test scaffolding, and common implementation patterns.

However, generated code should be treated as a proposed implementation rather than an automatically approved solution.

Examine the code for correctness, readability, algorithmic efficiency, type safety, security, and maintainability.

Developers should also check whether the implementation introduces unnecessary dependencies or unexpected side effects.

Use appropriate engineering tools to evaluate the generated implementation.

For Python projects, these might include:

These tools provide additional evidence about code quality, although none can independently guarantee correctness.

Before merging or deploying AI-assisted code, developers should be able to explain:

If developers cannot explain the behavior of a critical implementation, additional investigation is necessary.

As AI coding systems become more capable, the responsibilities of developers may continue to evolve.

Some implementation tasks will become increasingly automated, but software engineering involves broader responsibilities than writing individual functions.

Developers must translate business requirements into technical specifications, design system architectures, evaluate trade-offs, manage dependencies, identify security risks, and ensure reliability.

These responsibilities require technical judgment.

Understanding algorithms, data structures, networking, databases, operating systems, and software architecture remains important because these concepts determine how software behaves in real environments.

AI literacy is also becoming an important engineering competency.

Developers should understand how to formulate effective prompts, evaluate generated code, recognize model limitations, and verify technical claims.

The relationship between AI and programming knowledge should therefore be complementary.

AI can accelerate implementation, but engineering expertise determines whether the resulting software is appropriate, secure, efficient, and maintainable.

Programming education can also benefit from this approach. An AI programming tutor can provide explanations, exercises, and debugging guidance, while learners continue developing their own problem-solving abilities through practical coding. The broader approach to AI-assisted programming learning is most useful when AI guidance is combined with independent experimentation and technical evaluation.

The objective is not to avoid AI-generated code. It is to develop the ability to understand, evaluate, modify, and improve that code.

AI coding assistants are becoming valuable components of modern software development. They can reduce repetitive work, accelerate prototyping, explain unfamiliar code, and help developers explore alternative implementations.

However, code generation is only one part of software engineering.

Developers must still understand computational complexity, data structures, concurrency, type systems, testing strategies, security principles, and system architecture. These concepts provide the foundation for evaluating whether generated code actually solves the intended problem.

A working implementation is not necessarily an efficient implementation. Passing unit tests does not guarantee security. Syntactically correct code does not automatically satisfy architectural or business requirements.

These distinctions make programming knowledge more important, not less.

The most effective use of AI is not to eliminate the need for developers to understand code, but to help them work more efficiently while preserving their ability to reason about software.

AI should support programming knowledge, strengthen engineering judgment, and improve problem-solving capabilities. It should not replace the technical understanding required to build reliable software systems.

#9588. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Small English STT + LLM + TTS cascade with latency charts

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9587. In Security, Words Matter as Much as Tools — Maybe More

From talking cloud security to using AI, cyber leaders are finding that clear, disciplined communication is now a front-line defense capability across the enterprise.

The best tool cyber teams can wield to defend their organizations has nothing to do with tech; it's how they talk. Whether the audience is the C-suite, the development team, or the sheepish user who just fell for a phish, communications savvy is increasingly mission-critical.

During a Dark Reading Virtual Event panel I recently put together to talk tech, tools, integration, and frameworks, called "Key Tools & Technologies for Locking Down Your Cloud," SANS instructor Ahmed AbuGharbia urged cybersecurity teams to "learn the language of the cloud" to build credibility with IT, and to do the same for developers. We discussed technology and products, too, but I was surprised at the amount of time that was spent on stressing the importance of communication and language when it comes to having effective conversations with vendors, executives, and users.

My other panelist, Theresa Lanowitz, a principal analyst at Omdia, detailed the distinction between security "of" the cloud and security "in" the cloud, noting that under existing shared responsibility models, cloud service providers assume responsibility "of" the cloud itself, rather than what organizations decide to put "in" the cloud.

Related:US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

This wasn't the first time I had noticed a shift in the way security practitioners focus on a commitment to using effective language.

A couple of weeks ago I sat in several sessions at the ISC2 Strategic Conference in Denver that spent a remarkable amount of time on strategies for clearly communicating risk and documenting those exchanges in much the same way as they would any other log, piece of evidence, or asset. In the past, these conversations would have been more focused on translating tech talk into corporate speak. CISOs have worked for a long time on how to talk to leadership about risk and budget; it's been an ongoing conversation for several years. However, emphasis on how cyber teams can learn to ask the right questions not just of leadership, but pertinent people both inside and outside the business, feels like a fresh effort. Using precise language and presenting strategic (not just technical and tactical) concepts effectively is no longer being discussed as a nice thing for security pros to be able to do, but critical to fundamental enterprise defense.

For example, CISO and expert Laura Vaughn has cleverly broken down threat modeling into 4 Simple Questions on a White Board. Her strategy distills years of experience and technical expertise into plain language anyone can understand, like, "What [cyber incident] would hurt most on Monday morning?" That honed language helps get teams to the heart of the threats, and helps them understand the work that needs to happen next. That all saves time and money, and eliminates the scariest risks first. Other deceptively simple questions she suggests asking include, "Who hacks organizations like ours and how?" And, "What is the cheapest control?" Smart comms informs and focuses the technical work.

Related:Behind the Alias: How One Researcher Unmasked a Decade of Ransomware Actors

Likewise, technologist and attorney Daniel B. Garrie, CEO of Law and Forensics, presents language as a frontline defense, and coaches CISOs and cyber leaders on the finer points of contract negotiations. He advocates rigorous documentation of communications on risk and defense decisions, so those decisions would be defensible later, and so that transparency can help drive cybersecurity across the organization.

The introduction of AI is also requiring cybersecurity teams to pick their words carefully. AI has put a language interface between the user and compute operations that benefits those who can ask the best questions. Likewise, experts across the cyber sector urge caution around using humanizing language to describe AI agents or attribute human motivation to their actions.

Related:Why Holiday Security Can't Wait for Black Friday

Being an expert communicator is no longer a skill that's nice to have in cybersecurity; it's fundamental to enterprise defense. Be precise in the words you choose, and meet your audiences where they are. You might be surprised to find it's becoming the most powerful tool you or your organization could ever deploy against the next threat.

#9585. Verra Raises $5M From Kearny Jackson to Bring AI Agents to the $1.1T Consulting Industry

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

Global management consulting is a $1.1 trillion industry whose largest firms have committed billions of dollars to AI since 2023, from Accenture's $3 billion to KPMG's $2 billion. What those firms sell is expertise, yet a new engagement usually starts with a junior analyst searching old decks and past projects, because knowledge workers spend about 19% of their time searching for and gathering information.

Verra, a New York startup that builds an institutional memory layer for consulting firms, has raised a $5 million seed round led by Kearny Jackson, with participation from Petra, a16z speedrun and strategic angel investors. Founded in December 2025, the company reached seven-figure revenue within seven months of commercial launch and now runs across Berkeley Research Group, where 1,000 people use it to start client work from the firm's best previous thinking.

Consulting revenue has grown about 3.6% a year since 2020 to reach $1.1 trillion in 2025, while the industry is now rebuilding itself around AI. The Big Four have committed more than $10 billion to AI since 2023, with EY putting $1.4 billion into its EY.ai platform and PwC $1 billion into generative AI over three years.

The money is already reshaping the work. About 20% of BCG's 2024 revenue, or $2.7 billion of $13.5 billion, came from AI-related advisory, while McKinsey says 40% of its client work now involves AI. Firms that sell expertise are learning that their most valuable AI asset is the record of what they have already done for clients, which no outside model has seen.

A new engagement rarely starts from the firm's best work. Someone searches through old decks and previous projects, pieces together whatever turns up and rebuilds the deliverable for the new client, a process that takes about 80 hours to reach a first draft. Research from the McKinsey Global Institute found that interaction workers spend 19% of their week searching for and gathering information, or about 1.8 hours a day.

At firm scale, those hours add up fast. For a firm of 1,000 consultants working 2,000 hours a year, 19% comes to about 380,000 hours a year spent looking for information (our arithmetic). The first wave of AI tools helped with parts of the problem, since they could retrieve documents or generate text, but someone still had to turn that output into a working model or a client-ready deck.

Verra runs inside the firm's own cloud and learns from the proposals, models, reports and deliverables the firm has already produced. It distils how each practice works into reusable skills, which are packaged ways of doing a task the way that practice does it, then gives AI agents that context to produce new client work directly inside Word, Excel and PowerPoint.

An agent can find the relevant precedent, build the analysis, create the model and turn it into a presentation while linking every claim back to the page, cell or source it came from. Permissions mirror the firm's existing structure, so consultants only see files they could already open, while the platform carries SOC 2 Type II certification and offers a single-tenant deployment inside the firm's own cloud.

Across Verra's deployments, the time to a first draft of a client deliverable falls from roughly 80 hours to between 10 and 15 hours. That is 81% to 88% less time, or a draft five to eight times faster (our arithmetic), with the firm's best previous thinking built in from the first hour.

The saving matters because of how consulting is priced and staffed. Hours that used to go into rebuilding a starting point can go into analysis, client conversations and judgment, which is the work clients pay senior people for. The sources attached to every claim also shorten review, since a manager can check where a number came from without redoing the research.

Berkeley Research Group, a global consulting firm working in corporate finance, economics, disputes and investigations, rolled Verra out to 1,000 people within two months of a proof of concept, driven by demand from inside the firm. Verra now runs across BRG under the firm's own brand. Since August, its consultants have used it to generate 105,000 files and make 145,000 edits directly inside open Office documents.

That works out to about 920 files and 1,270 edits a day. Among onboarded teams, more than 87% of consultants use Verra every week, while BRG estimates the savings at thousands of analyst hours a week. The Keystone Group, one of Verra's first customers, has also deployed it firmwide.

Verra was founded in December 2025 by Kashyap Nathan, its CEO, who previously worked at OpenAI and Palantir, together with Christopher Farrington, who previously worked at Deloitte. The two started the company after watching consultants repeatedly search for work their own firms had already completed.

They built the product around three facts about professional services. Client data cannot leave the firm, so Verra runs inside the customer's cloud. Consultants will not trust an answer they cannot verify, so every output carries its sources. AI does not get adopted if it forces people out of the tools they already use, so Verra works inside Office files, while the company's engineers build practice-specific workflows inside each firm in days.

Their wider view is that AI will make raw intelligence cheap and widely available, which leaves a firm's own record of decades of client work as the advantage that is hardest to copy. Verra's goal is to make that knowledge compound, so each engagement leaves the firm smarter for the next one.

The $5 million seed round is led by Kearny Jackson, with participation from Petra, a16z speedrun and strategic angel investors. Verra will use the money to accelerate product development, hire and build integrations with the enterprise knowledge systems that consulting firms already run.

The round comes less than a year after founding and after the company had already reached seven-figure revenue, mostly through adoption that spread inside customers once it landed. That pattern, with a product pulled into new practice groups by the consultants using it, is the core of the case investors are backing.

Kearny Jackson is a San Francisco seed firm co-founded by Sriram Krishnan, a former product manager at Tinder and Spotify, together with Sunil Chhaya, previously at Menlo Ventures and Tenaya Capital. Its $65 million Fund III counts Marc Andreessen and Sequoia among its limited partners, while its portfolio includes MotherDuck, Cortex, Comulate and EigenLayer.

Krishnan, who has worked in consulting, points to how much consulting time goes into rinse-and-repeat work because a firm's knowledge is hard to reuse. What stood out to the firm was how quickly Verra became critical inside the firms using it, with consultants adopting it and asking for more. Kearny Jackson's view is that Verra is becoming the memory and operating layer for how consulting firms work, a position that grows more valuable with every engagement it records.

Verra plans to expand from individual practices into firmwide intelligence, then into adjacent sectors including accounting, advisory and investment research. It will also let customer engineering teams build on top of the platform without recreating the underlying infrastructure themselves.

If AI makes general intelligence a commodity, the firms that win will be the ones that remember best. Verra is building for that world, where every consultant starts each engagement with everything the firm has ever learned already at work.

#9584. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

#9583. Customer Churn Prediction Is More Than Picking a Model

I am an applied AI & data analytics practitioner focused on building real-world machine learning solutions

I am an applied AI & data analytics practitioner focused on building real-world machine learning solutions

I am an applied AI & data analytics practitioner focused on building real-world machine learning solutions

When I started working on customer churn prediction, it was tempting to focus on the model: try Logistic Regression, try Random Forest, then compare the scores.

But a model is only one part of the work. Before training anything, you need to decide what “churn” means, check that the data makes sense and choose a way to evaluate the model that reflects the problem you’re trying to solve.

Here’s the workflow I use to think through a churn project in Python.

“Churn” can mean different things depending on the business. For a subscription service, it might mean a customer cancelled. For another product, it could mean that a customer stopped buying or using the service for a set period.

That definition affects the whole project, so it’s worth making it explicit.

There’s also a timing question: when are you trying to make the prediction? If you want to identify customers who might leave next month, your features should only include information that would have been available before that month. Including information recorded after a customer leaves can make a model look better than it really is.

Churn datasets often mix numerical columns, such as tenure or monthly charges, with categories like contract type or payment method. Those need slightly different treatment.

Here’s a basic scikit-learn setup. It fills missing values, scales numerical features and encodes categorical ones. In this example, the target column is called Churn; change that if your dataset uses a different name.

Keeping preprocessing inside a pipeline is helpful because the transformations are fitted on the training data, not on the entire dataset before the split.

For a straightforward experiment, I’d start with a stratified train-test split. Stratification helps keep a similar proportion of churn and non-churn cases in each set.

A random split isn’t right for every project. If the records are time-based, it may be more realistic to train on earlier data and test on later data. The split should reflect how you expect the model to be used.

Logistic Regression is a reasonable place to start. It gives you a baseline without making the first version of the project more complicated than it needs to be.

Accuracy can be misleading when fewer customers churn than stay. A model that predicts “stay” for almost everyone might still get a decent accuracy score while missing many of the customers you wanted to identify.

The confusion matrix gives you a more concrete view of those mistakes. Precision and recall help describe the trade-off between incorrectly flagging customers and missing customers who do churn. ROC-AUC shows how well the model ranks churn cases above non-churn cases across different thresholds, but it doesn’t tell you which threshold to use.

Many classifiers use 0.5 as the default threshold for turning a probability into a yes-or-no prediction. That’s a starting point, not a rule.

If the business wants to reach as many potential churners as possible, it may accept more false alarms. If contacting customers is costly or could annoy them, it may prefer to flag fewer people with greater confidence.

The choice depends on what happens after the prediction. I’d choose a threshold using validation data and the needs of the intended use, rather than repeatedly adjusting it based on the test results.

A model can show that certain features are associated with churn. That doesn’t prove those features caused it.

For example, if customers on a particular type of contract are more likely to churn in the data, the contract might not be the underlying reason. Other factors, such as tenure, pricing or service experience, could be involved.

I treat model results as clues to investigate, not as a complete explanation of a customer’s behaviour.

For a portfolio project, the notebook or repository should explain the choices, not just show the final score. I’d include:

That makes the project more useful to someone reviewing it and makes it easier to reproduce later.

The main lesson for me is that churn prediction isn’t just a contest between classifiers. The definition of the problem, the timing of the data and the way the results are evaluated all matter. A model is useful only when those choices make sense for the task.

#9581. Building a Sales Forecast That’s Useful Beyond the Model Score

I am an applied AI & data analytics practitioner focused on building real-world machine learning solutions

I am an applied AI & data analytics practitioner focused on building real-world machine learning solutions

I am an applied AI & data analytics practitioner focused on building real-world machine learning solutions

A sales forecast can look convincing on a chart and still be difficult to use.

The model might produce numbers for the next six months, but a business also needs to know how those numbers were produced, how uncertain they are and whether the evaluation reflects the way the forecast will actually be used.

In a retail forecasting project, I worked through monthly sales aggregation, time-based features and a comparison between Linear Regression and Random Forest. Here’s how I approach the process, and the checks I’d make before relying on the result.

Before choosing a model, be clear about what you’re forecasting. Is it total sales for the business, sales for each product, or sales by store and month? The answer determines how the data should be grouped.

It’s also useful to ask how far ahead the forecast needs to go. Predicting next month’s sales is a different task from forecasting six months ahead. As the forecast horizon grows, uncertainty usually becomes more important to communicate.

Sales data often starts at the transaction level. For a monthly forecast, the first step is to aggregate it by month.

This assumes the file has columns called date and sales. Use the actual column names in your dataset. Also check for missing months, duplicate records and unusual values before fitting a model. A zero-sales month might be real, or it might mean the data was missing.

Calendar features such as month number can help a model learn seasonal patterns. Lag features can capture recent sales history, but they must be created carefully: a forecast for a given month can only use values that would have been available at the time.

Here, lag_1 is the previous month’s sales, and lag_12 is sales from the same month a year earlier. Those features can be helpful when the data has enough history, but they are not automatically useful for every dataset.

A random train-test split can mix future observations into the training set. For forecasting, that can give an overly optimistic evaluation.

A simple approach is to train on earlier months and test on the most recent months:

For a more thorough evaluation, use rolling time-based validation. Train on an initial period, test on the next period, then move the cutoff forward and repeat. That helps show whether the model performs consistently across different periods.

Linear Regression can provide an understandable starting point. A Random Forest can capture nonlinear patterns, but it may not extrapolate trends well beyond the values it has seen.

It’s also worth comparing both against a simple baseline, such as predicting that next month will be the same as the previous month. A more complex model should earn its place by doing better on data it did not train on.

No single metric tells the whole story. Mean absolute error is easy to interpret in the same units as sales. Root mean squared error gives more weight to large errors. Percentage-based metrics can be difficult to interpret when actual sales are zero or close to zero.

A metric should be considered alongside a plot of actual and predicted values. That makes it easier to notice whether the model consistently misses peaks, lags behind a trend or performs poorly during particular periods.

A forecast is not a promise about what will happen. Promotions, stock availability, price changes and unexpected events can all affect sales, and a model may not know about them.

When sharing a forecast, explain the period it covers, the data used, the evaluation method and any important limitations. If possible, show a range or scenario alongside the central estimate rather than presenting one line as certainty.

A useful sales forecast is not just the model with the best score. It is a forecast built with the right time boundaries, compared against a simple baseline and explained in a way that helps people make decisions.

#9580. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997

Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

"Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.

Nobody thinks that, literally. What I mean by that is, nothing capable of thinking would have written this sentence down because no thinking entity would suspect that decision models originated probabilistic classification. Only a non-thinking source of language, such as an LLM, might generate this sentence.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Again, nobody thinks that, meaning only an LLM might generate this sentence.

The state + questions interface carries over to hosted decision models too. meraGPT Decider 1.1 takes the same shape through an API (model decider-1.1) rather than as open weights: up to 255 options per choice question, images in the state, and if you offer an "I don't know" option it takes it when the state doesn't support an answer. Against TypeSafe Jev 1.14 on the same items it's ahead on typed decisions, calibration and large label sets. Input is $0.04 per million tokens and output is free.

Release notes: https://meragpt.com/blog/introducing-decider-1-1?utm_source=huggingface&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=hf_decision_blog

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

#9578. The Hidden Engineering Work Behind a Paid Media Experiment

A campaign test can look simple on a slide: change a setting, compare the results and keep the winner.

The difficult part is making sure the comparison tells you what you think it tells you.

If the test and control groups were different to begin with, if other changes happened at the same time, or if the team decides what counts as success after seeing the results, the conclusion may be less reliable than the chart suggests.

“Improve performance” is too vague to guide an experiment. A useful hypothesis names the change and the outcome.

Does reducing campaign exposure in selected regions lower media spend without materially reducing completed purchases?

That gives the team a testable question. It also makes it easier to agree on what should remain unchanged.

Choose the primary outcome before the test begins. It might be completed purchases, qualified leads or contribution margin. Clicks and platform-attributed conversions can help explain what happened, but they may not answer whether the test created business value.

Every experiment needs something that can be assigned to the test or control condition. Depending on the account and available tools, that might be a geographic area, an audience segment or a time period.

Decide on the unit before launching. Changing it after looking at early results makes the comparison harder to interpret.

A written experiment record prevents details from being reconstructed from memory later. It doesn’t need to be a long document, but it should capture the hypothesis, test and control conditions, outcome, dates and known limitations.

Save the relevant campaign settings at the start of the test. If the test later produces an unexpected result, the team can check whether the setup changed.

If budget, targeting, creative and landing pages all change during the same test, the result may show that something changed without revealing which change mattered.

Keep the experiment focused where possible. If a promotion, inventory issue or product change cannot be avoided, record it. That context may explain why the results moved.

Conversion delay matters too. A person may click during the test period but purchase later. Ending the test before the normal customer journey has had time to complete can understate the outcome.

Raw conversion totals can be misleading when the test and control groups differ in size. A rate or another normalised measure may provide a fairer comparison.

Outcome rate=eligible unitsqualifying outcomes​

The right statistical method depends on the test design, data volume and outcome type. A small test can show a sizeable difference that is still too uncertain to support a strong conclusion.

That result is not necessarily a failure. “Inconclusive” means the evidence was not sufficient to make a confident call. It does not prove that the campaign had no effect.

Teams can be tempted to call a test successful when one metric improves, even if another important outcome worsens. Set the decision rule before reviewing results.

For example, decide in advance whether the test must reduce spend, maintain a minimum level of qualified outcomes and meet a profitability threshold. The exact rule should reflect the business objective, not a convenient result discovered afterwards.

If estimated business value is included, make the assumptions visible. A conversion count is not the same as profit, and a short test may not support a precise value estimate.

Platform reports are useful for understanding delivery and attribution. They don’t automatically represent the total business impact of an experiment.

Where appropriate, compare outcomes with a business source of truth such as a CRM or order system. Check that the test and control use the same outcome definition and that duplicate records are handled consistently.

If platform and business-system numbers differ, investigate the definitions, reporting periods and processing delays before drawing conclusions.

A useful readout includes the original hypothesis, test design, dates, outcome definition, results, relevant changes and limitations. It should also explain the decision and the evidence behind it.

This record helps the next person understand whether the result applies to the same campaign, audience or market. It also stops the team from repeating an experiment without knowing what was learned last time.

The engineering work behind a paid media experiment is mostly about definitions, assignment, data consistency and change control. Get those pieces right, and even a modest test can provide useful evidence. Skip them, and a polished chart may only show that two things happened at the same time.
